News.title: 'If that means I lose my job, so be it': Top Fifa official questions Infantino's World Cup plan
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino's position came under further scrutiny on Friday as the governing body's chief operating officer strongly criticised his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.

In a statement released to the Associated Press, Kevin Lamour described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and said "the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions".

The lengthy statement did not mention Infantino by name.

It came on the same day a third confederation spoke out against the plans, a senior adviser to Infantino resigned, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Swiss was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.

US President Donald Trump - addressing the proposals for the first time - said he had not spoken to Infantino about the plans.

The two have developed a close relationship since Trump assumed office for a second time in 2025.

Lamour said in his statement: "Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football.

"A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite."

Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues.

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he added. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

News.title: Disgraced funeral boss who failed to bury bodies jailed for 20 years
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

The court heard Bush defrauded nearly 200 families out of Â£562,117 and had acted out of "financial greed".

Hilliard warned that unless a body was one of those recovered by police in 2024 and properly identified, no-one who had used Legacy's cremations services "at any time can be absolutely certain they received the ashes of their loved one".

"He must have a heartless side to him - which allowed him to treat the living and the dead in the way he did, and he was very confident he would get away with what he was doing."

The judge added: "I don't think I have ever known offences affecting so many people and so deeply."

The court was told relatives of 46 people who were cremated between 2017 and 2024 were given the wrong ashes and the loved ones of another 11 never received any.

"How betrayed they now feel," said the judge.

"Husbands and wives, partners, parents, children, grandchildren, now discovering that they are left with nothing, or in some cases we heard, an empty plastic bag or a teaspoonful of ash which the police managed to recover for them."

News.title: England and Wales on course for driest July on record
News.content:
England and Wales are on course for their driest July since records began 190 years ago.

The Met Office reports that England has seen just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it is 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

The UK as a whole is currently on track for its third driest July, and driest nationally since 1868.

News.title: Passenger on British Airways mayday flight describes fear and shout of 'I don't want to die'
News.content:
A passenger on a British Airways flight that issued a distress call on approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month has described the rising fear in the cabin and a lack of information from the crew.

Edward Killiwick had been travelling back from a friend's birthday party with his partner Julie, on the flight from Dusseldorf in Germany on 6 July.

He said passengers were told that the landing had been aborted, and then he felt a "very violent manoeuvre" and "did think we could crash". He and his partner had to comfort a woman who "completely lost it and started screaming, 'I don't want to die'".

The flight landed safely, but the incident is being investigated with assistance from BA.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident", and France's accident investigation authority, the BEA, said on Wednesday that the plane, an Airbus A320, had issued a distress call.

Edward said: "The violent manoeuvre almost felt like it was avoiding another aircraft. You could feel the engines going at full power.

"It was a bit odd going around in a holding pattern with no information. I thought if they're not talking, then they're not in a good place."

He said they were in a holding pattern for about 15 minutes.

The BEA said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet â which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

Edward said: "I was definitely scared. After the violent manoeuvre I thought, there is definitely something very badly wrong here. I did think we could crash.

"I did think it was a possibility, and I think everyone else did."

News.title: Parents sue school over 'inhumane' calming rooms after BBC report
News.content:
Parents are suing a special school after a BBC investigation uncovered CCTV footage showing autistic children being locked inside calming rooms and abused.

Ten families are claiming that their children â all of whom had learning disabilities or several mental disorders - were amongst those harmed by their treatment in the rooms.

A police investigation into the abuse, recorded inside the rooms at Whitefield special school in north London, ended two years ago without any charges.

The school is now run by a new trust which says the failings have led to "important learning".

Many special schools use seclusion spaces such as calming rooms outside of classrooms to address sensory needs or challenging behaviour.

But the leaked footage obtained by the BBC showed children being shoved into padded rooms, thrown to the floor, restrained by the neck - or left alone, sitting in vomit.

One 12-year-old boy appeared in over 55 hours of CCTV footage filmed inside the rooms.

At the time, the Children's Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, said the use of the rooms was "horrifying".

Leigh Day is now bringing a civil legal claim on behalf of 10 families against the trust which ran the school and the London borough of Waltham Forest.

The law firm says the use of the rooms was "barbaric", according to its clients. The claim alleges that children were falsely imprisoned and their human rights were breached.

"What was done to these children was profoundly harmful, and its impact continues to be felt by families every day", says Alison Millar, who is leading the case.

The CCTV obtained by the BBC had been recorded between 2014 and 2017 but only emerged in 2021.

Last month, a long-delayed review commissioned by Waltham Forest found that restraint and seclusion became "normalised" and a culture developed that allowed "pejorative views of non-compliant children".

It added that parents were clear that the practices were "unimaginable" and "inhumane".

The BBC has also found evidence of mistreatment in seclusion rooms at other schools across the UK.

CCTV from a different school showed a boy being "brutally" and "unlawfully" restrained, while elsewhere an autistic child was kept inside a cage.

News.title: Burnham faces criticism over plans for mayors to get share of income tax
News.content:
The government is facing criticism over its plan to allow regional mayors to keep a share of income tax and business rates in England.

Andy Burnham says that the proposals, expected to be phased in from next April, will give metro mayors powers to invest the money in their communities for public services.

The prime minister said on Friday that this amounted to "the biggest shift of power out of Whitehall and Westminster" to regions across the UK.

But Lord Houchen, the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley, argues he should be able to offer taxpayers a rebate instead, while opposition parties say the plans could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out.

"The prime minister has said he wants to alleviate the cost of living [crisis] and give people room to breathe - what better way to do that than allow them to keep more of their own money?" the Tory mayor told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told the BBC that there was not currently a mechanism in place for mayors to offer a rebate.

But Lord Houchen said it was "not beyond the wit of man" to create a system, adding it would not be "overly complicated" and would not be particularly controversial.

"I think the prime minister and what this government is doing on fiscal devolution is a move in the right direction, but for it to be real devolution we've got to have local decision-making and choose what's best for the people we represent."

Burnham later directly rejected the idea of mayors giving their taxpayers rebates, telling reporters the plans were not about making local leaders into "mini-chancellors of the exchequer, undermining or rewriting policy on tax and personal finance".

As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding by central government grants.

Mayors are expected to start retaining some revenue from business rates from April 2027 and receive a portion of income tax from April 2028.

The rates of income tax will not change as a result of the reform.

Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, has made devolution a centrepiece of his agenda in the early weeks of his premiership.

He said this policy would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

Chancellor John Healey will set out more of the detail when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October.

News.title: Puberty blockers trial can start recruiting children after judge rejects legal challenge
News.content:
A high-profile clinical trial of drugs that can delay puberty in children questioning their gender can go ahead after the High Court rejected a legal challenge by campaigners.

The Pathways trial, run by researchers at King's College London (KCL), will start recruiting more than 220 children aged between 11 and 16 years old from 1 August.

The study was commissioned to assess the benefits or risks of puberty blockers, after a landmark review into gender services found the evidence for treating young people with the drugs was "remarkably weak".

Campaigners who brought the legal action had argued the safeguards in place were inadequate and raised concerns about the long-term physical and psychological effects on young people.

The judge, Mr Justice Chamberlain, refused the application for a judicial review saying that none of the claims made by the campaigners had a realistic chance of success.

He said that each patient involved in the trial will have been assessed over "many months" by specialist doctors who will have "formed the opinion that a child has a reasonable prospect of receiving a clinical benefit from the treatment".

A spokeswoman for KCL welcomed the court's decision, saying the "safety and welfare of young people will remain our highest priority in carrying out this research".

Campaigners, including parents of gender-questioning children, said they were disappointed by the decision saying the "world is watching" a case which has "global implications and high stakes".

News.title: Southport killer charged with prison attacks and possessing weapon
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been charged with three attacks while in prison and possessing a weapon.

Police say the offences took place at HMP Belmarsh over six months from May to October 2025.

The 19-year-old murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year sentence in January 2025. Earlier this month he was moved to a secure psychiatric hospital.

Rudakubana is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court remotely on 11 September.

He has been charged with the following four offences:

Assault on an emergency worker on 6 May 2025

Attempted grievous bodily harm on 8 May 2025

Unauthorised possession of an offensive weapon in prison on 26 June 2025

Assault on an emergency worker on 28 October 2025

In May 2025, it was reported boiling water had been thrown on a prison officer at Belmarsh. They were taken to hospital and discharged on the same day.

When Rudakubana was jailed, the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to him being under-18 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

On 23 July, the MoJ confirmed Rudakubana was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The decision to transfer him was criticised by a lawyer representing the families of victims.

News.title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.

Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.

The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.

Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.

But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country".

"Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told BBC Radio 4's Today programme areas without mayors would also benefit from investment because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.

Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.

But Labour backbencher Perran Moon said the government's plans were "discriminatory" and could create a "two-tier system".

The MP for Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall said the area would never have a mayor or become a combined authority and so risked not having access to devolved powers that other areas would have.

"What we're asking government to do is to provide us with the same powers, the same funding that mayoral combined authorities have without the requirement of becoming a combined authority or having a mayor."

The government has also announced that mayors will be given a fast-track route to building new tramways, roads and light rail in their areas.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the threshold at which local leaders need to seek approval for projects will rise to Â£500m, up from Â£200m.

News.title: Budget to be held in October, Healey announces
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has announced the date of his first Budget will be Wednesday, 28 October.

In aâ¯video message,â¯ he said: "This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.

"It will be built on fiscal discipline. It will meet our fiscal rules. It'll give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future. Now, let's get on with the job."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

Burnham also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain shouldl lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

But questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

News.title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
News.content:
Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for Â£120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.

Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.

The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.

There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.

Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.

The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.

Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.

Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.

Sainsbury's bought Argos â together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group â in 2016 for Â£1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around Â£720m in 2024.

In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.

Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Roberts said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.

He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat products

Swift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".

The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.

Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops â and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.

News.title: Thames Water boss says leakage targets 'not realistic'
News.content:
Water companies have performance commitments on issues such as leakage.

It is illegal to release raw sewage into rivers and seas during "normal" weather conditions, but firms are allowed to do so when it rains heavily, to prevent homes being flooded.

Thames is the UK's largest water company, supplying water and wastewater services to 16 million customers across London and parts of southern England.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Weston said the company treats 4.3 billion litres of waste a day, and "99.5% of the time" it gets treated successfully, although "sometimes something goes wrong".

"We want to do better when it comes to pollutions," he said, but added, "the targets that the company is expected to make are not realistic.

"[For example], we have to hit a certain level of leakage, but it is so far in excess of what we are capable of doing, I think anyone would be capable of doing, however much money you invested, that it is not going to be achievable."

The chance of getting to zero pollution was "very, very slim", he added.

Ofwat told the BBC: "With around a fifth of water put into supply still lost through leakage, companies must deliver on the commitments they have been funded to achieve.

"Water company targets are intended to be ambitious and drive better outcomes for customers and the environment."

A spokesperson for the Environment Agency said: "[We] and the public expect Thames Water to comply with the law," adding that the agency would continue to hold companies to account where performance falls short.

James Wallace, chief executive of campaign group River Action, said: "Thames Water's tactics of opacity and deflection fool no-one. Telling the public to save water while this wasteful profit-obsessed corporation leaks 570 million litres of treated drinking water every day is offensive.

"There is nothing 'realistic' about accepting sewage pollution as inevitable. The choice is simple: keep propping up a failed privatised financial model, or put Thames Water into special administration and rebuild it as a public utility serving customers, rivers and the public."

News.title: Residents hit by flooding call for quarry to shut after blast
News.content:
Residents who were forced to evacuate their homes because of flooding following a planned blast at Taff's Well quarry have called for it to shut.

Emergency services were called and roads remain shut in Gwaelod-y-Garth on the outskirts of Cardiff, with around 40 people "directly affected" according to the city's council leader Chris Weaver.

A spokesperson for the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) said it would work with South Wales Police to investigate.

The chief executive officer of quarry owner the Breedon Group, Mike Pearce, said it would support the authorities with their investigation and would be carrying out its own to understand what happened.

One resident facing a major home clean-up said the blast was so noticeable that "the whole house shook like a bomb had gone off", while another said it had been like three times the usual "mini earthquake".

News.title: High Court upholds decision to allow Chinese mega embassy
News.content:
A High Court challenge against the construction of a Chinese mega embassy in London has failed.

The decision to uphold planning permission for the site on the old Royal Mint, near the Tower of London, has dismayed campaigners from the Royal Mint Court Residents' Association (RMCRA), which represents families and businesses in about 100 properties.

The RMCRA fear the site poses an espionage threat and will be used to enforce "draconian" Chinese laws in the UK and to target dissidents.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) and the London Borough of Tower Hamlets defended the claim, saying they "conscientiously and carefully had regard" to the residents' concerns.

The association was also concerned about the Chinese government creating a fire risk by ignoring safety obligations, which it said would not be enforceable because of diplomatic immunity.

A High Court hearing was held earlier this month and two judges have now dismissed RMCRA's challenge.

Mrs Justice Lieven, sitting with Lord Justice Dingemans, said there was "no doubt" that the government took into account that it was the Chinese government applying for planning permission.

She also said that the RMCRA was not disadvantaged by not receiving a copy of a "blast assessment" at the time of the planning decision, which detailed the effect of a possible terrorist explosion.

The judge said: "There was no unfairness to the claimant by reason of these documents not having been disclosed."

Speaking outside Parliament, Luke de Pulford of the Interparliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), who has been supporting the RMCRA, confirmed solicitors had been instructed to appeal against the High Court ruling, funded by donations from the public.

RMCRA spokesman Mark Nygate said residents believed this was only an early skirmish in the battle against the mega embassy.

"We knew this was going to be a long haul and we intend to go all the way... as far as the Supreme Court," he said.

"This is a huge case with consequences that go far beyond planning law, far beyond the residents, far from the local community - this is about our country."

News.title: British man accused of spying on Cyprus RAF base for Iran
News.content:
A British man has been arrested on suspicion of spying on a UK military base in Cyprus on behalf of the Iranian military.

Rashad Sultanov, 44, of Islington, north London, is accused of carrying out "hostile surveillance" on RAF Akrotiri and sharing information with the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

Sultanov, who also holds Azerbaijani citizenship, was arrested by Cypriot police on 17 July and is in custody pending extradition proceedings.

The Crown Prosecution Service has said he will be charged under the National Security Act - the first time an alleged offence under the 2023 law has been investigated in an overseas territory.

News.title: World Cup boycott latest: Trump claims he didn’t speak to Infantino about sell-off plans as pressure mounts on Fifa boss
News.content:
Inside Uefa’s extraordinary World Cup boycott plans – and what Fifa might do next

Gianni Infantino is under mounting pressure from football federations as well as from within Fifa after Uefa’s boycott of the World Cup left his plans to privatise its tournaments in tatters.

Infantino’s long-term adviser Carlos Cordeiro, a key figure within Fifa, has quit in protest of Infantino’s proposals, while Fifa’s chief operating officer has said that Infantino “deceived” staff over his plans. The Asian Football Confederation, meanwhile, has become the third federation to reject them publicly, releasing a strong statement on Friday backing the stance of Uefa and Concacaf, while claiming that confidence in Fifa’s governance has been “undermined”.

Donald Trump meanwhile told reporters on Friday that he has not spoken to Infantino about the plans despite their close relationship and the fact that Josh Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is expected to lead ⁠the proposed investor group.

Earlier Fifa hit back at Uefa, insisting that “nobody is selling football” and confirming that it will continue its consultation period ahead of a vote on 19 September. But after another federation joined Uefa’s side, Infantino looks unlikely to get the votes he needs and is instead facing growing opposition to his leadership.

On Thursday, Uefa announced that it would boycott the World Cup and all Fifa competitions if Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its major tournaments to external investors are voted through.

News.title: 12 best dry shampoos that keep hair fresh between washes
News.content:
Your questions about dry shampoo answered

What is the best dry shampoo?

After weeks of testing, K18’s airwash emerged as the best dry shampoo, even with its sky-high price taken into account. Unlike traditional powder-heavy formulas, its liquid spray left both of our heads of hair feeling freshly washed and without the stiffness, chalkiness or scalp build-up that so often comes with dry shampoos. We were both impressed by how little product was needed, how weightless it felt and how effectively it revived oily roots while adding moveable volume. Ultimately, all its many merits made the steep price tag feel easier to justify, especially given that one bottle lasted more than six months in testing.

Elsewhere, Batiste’s colour dry shampoo proved a reliable budget buy, Living Proof’s original PhD formula delivered the deepest clean, Sam McKnight’s lazy girl dry shampoo excelled on fine hair thanks to its undetectable texture, while Typebea’s scalp-focused formula stood out for its lightweight texture.

How we tested dry shampoos

To find the best dry shampoos, I tested a wide range of aerosols, liquid sprays and powder applicators across several months (and, in some cases, years), assessing how well they refreshed oily roots, boosted volume and held up throughout the day.

I called on a tester with brunette hair to judge residue levels and blendability across deeper hues, while I focused on how the formulas fared on my fine, blonde hair prone to flattening, clumping and oiliness. Specifically, we took the following factors into consideration:

Oil absorption: We assessed how effectively each formula disguised greasy roots and whether hair looked noticeably cleaner after application.

We assessed how effectively each formula disguised greasy roots and whether hair looked noticeably cleaner after application. Texture: We considered whether the dry shampoo left strands soft and touchable or stiff, chalky and cloying

We considered whether the dry shampoo left strands soft and touchable or stiff, chalky and cloying White cast: We noted how visible each formula appeared on both blonde and brunette hair, and how easy it was to blend in.

We noted how visible each formula appeared on both blonde and brunette hair, and how easy it was to blend in. Volume: We tested whether formulas added noticeable lift and body, particularly at the roots and crown

We tested whether formulas added noticeable lift and body, particularly at the roots and crown Longevity: We monitored how long results lasted before hair began looking oily or flat again.

We monitored how long results lasted before hair began looking oily or flat again. Scent: We took into account the various dry shampoo fragrances, both immediately and, where applicable, as they developed throughout the day.

We took into account the various dry shampoo fragrances, both immediately and, where applicable, as they developed throughout the day. Ease of application: We considered how evenly the product dispersed and how convenient the packaging felt

We considered how evenly the product dispersed and how convenient the packaging felt Value for money: We weighed up performance against price, factoring in how much product was needed per use and how quickly bottles ran out.

What is the best dry shampoo for fine hair?

“For fine hair, you want a dry shampoo that refreshes the scalp without coating the strands too heavily,” reveals hair stylist Lorraine Dublin. Specifically, she suggests looking out for the following buzzwords on product packaging:

Lightweight

Invisible finish

Volume boosting

Weightless

She tells me about the ingredients fine hair types should keep an eye out for when shopping dry shampoos, particularly “rice starch and tapioca starch.”

“Try to avoid formulas with heavy oils, thick powders or overly fragranced ingredients, especially if your scalp is sensitive or prone to buildup,” she cautions.

“Personally, I love the pale Ouai dry shampoo and the Living Proof dry shampoo,” feeds in hair stylist Joe Kelly, “I use both regularly on clients because they give that airy, fluffy texture without making the hair feel sticky or overloaded with product.”

How to use dry shampoo

“You can use dry shampoo from the roots all the way through to the ends, depending on the effect you want to achieve,” advises Kelly.

Breaking down the different ways of using dry shampoo, he lists:

“If it’s just to absorb oil or grease, apply it mainly at the scalp and roots. A practical guideline would be around 2–3 sprays.”

“If you want texture, movement, and a more lived-in finish, spray it throughout the hair. Around 3-4 sprays.”

Expanding on Kelly’s advice, Dublin feeds in, “Massage the dry shampoo gently with your fingertips or brush through to evenly distribute the product. Let it sit for a minute or two so the product has time to absorb oil properly.”

“Applying dry shampoo the night before can actually work really well because it gives the product time to absorb oil overnight and leaves the hair looking fresher by morning,” she adds.

Is dry shampoo bad for hair?

“Dry shampoo itself is not bad for the hair when used correctly and in moderation,” clarifies Dublin. She continues, “The issue usually comes from overuse or not cleansing the scalp properly between applications.”

This is because, she elaborates, “A healthy scalp environment matters and dry shampoo should be seen as a styling and refresh product, not a replacement for washing the hair.”

Can dry shampoo cause hair loss?

“Dry shampoo doesn’t directly cause hair loss,” reassures Kelly, who tells me that “overusing it can irritate the scalp and contribute to issues like buildup, dryness, dandruff or breakage, especially if you already have a dry or sensitive scalp.”

Why you can trust IndyBest reviews

Lucy Smith is a senior shopping writer for IndyBest and is well versed on a number of haircare products, from the best shampoos and conditioners to the best hair brushes. She regularly speaks to hair stylists and trichologists to inform her reviews and, as someone who suffers with oily roots regularly, she was up to the task of testing the very best dry shampoos.

Daisy Lester was IndyBest’s senior shopping writer and has covered all manner of hair treatments, including the Olaplex no.3 plus perfector and the £5 gloss treatment to rival Color Wow’s dream coat. Daisy regularly attends new product launches and expert masterclasses, she’s across all the industry’s movers and shakers. Plus, she’s been using dry shampoos for years and – prior to testing, even – had a good gauge on which brands and formulas were the cream of the crop.

News.title: Tour de France Femmes 2026 stage-by-stage guide: Route maps and profiles for all 21 days
News.content:

The Tour de France Femmes returns for 2026 on Saturday with possibly the toughest edition yet of what has rapidly become the flagship race for women’s cycling.

Now in its fifth year, the 2026 race features just shy of 19,000m of elevation gain across 1,175km of largely hilly and testing terrain, with an individual time trial on the menu alongside an historic first trip up the legendary Tour climb of Mont Ventoux on stage seven, the race’s queen stage.

The nine-stage race, which begins with three days in Switzerland before crossing into France, could go right down to the wire with an explosive final stage in Nice featuring four climbs of the tough Col d’Eze crammed into less than 100km of racing.

Dutchwoman and 2023 champion Demi Vollering is arguably the favourite to regain her crown but will face fierce competition from reigning champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot, who has had a mixed season but with everything building towards her title defence.

2024 winner Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, who has finished on the podium in every edition, is another major contender, while the start list also features this year’s breakout star, Paula Blasi, former Giro d’Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini, and world time-trial champion Marlen Reusser.

Route guide

open image in gallery Tour de France Femmes 2026 route ( ASO )

Stage 1: Lausanne > Lausanne (138km, flat)

The race begins in Lausanne, Switzerland, with a parcours officially classified as ‘flat’ but actually rolling, heading north out of Lausanne and following the shores of the Lac de Neuchatel and Lac Leman. There are four categorised climbs and an uphill finish on the category four Côte Saint-François, which is 2.5km long at an average of 4.6%. The undulating terrain and drag to the line means any number of different types of rider could feature in the finale, which should make for a frantic first day of racing, and a reduced group sprint the most likely outcome.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 2: Aigle > Geneva (147.9km, flat)

Stage two is much more sprinter-friendly despite another five categorised hills along the way to a flat finish in Geneva, on the second of three days in Switzerland. The stage hugs the shores of Lake Geneva as it heads west away from Lausanne, with all the climbing in the first 100km and a largely flat final 40km, including the last 8km returning to the shore of Lac Leman, for the sprinters’ trains to get organised. Lorena Wiebes, as on every flat finish, is the favourite here.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 3: Geneva > Poligny (156.5km, hilly)

The hills return on a surprisingly tough stage three, with climbing straight out of the gate as the race leaves Geneva and enters France via the Jura mountains. The Col de la Faucille is the first and most brutal ascent of the day, a category one at 11.4km, averaging 6.3% and kicking off from the gun.

The category three Cote de Lajoux follows straight after the descent off the Faucille and there’s another two categorised climbs on an undulating parcours towards Poligny, before the climbing drops off entirely with the final 24km all flat or downhill. This could be one for a breakaway if enough riders can get organised on the difficult early climbs, or another bunch sprint.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 4: Gevrey-Chambertin > Dijon (21km, ITT)

After an absence from last year’s edition the individual time trial returns to the Tour de France Femmes; this is the first major test for the general classification contenders and a chance for the TT specialists to have their day in the sun. The first 7km wind their way through flat vineyards before a short but steep climb, the 1.8km Lacets de Marsannay, which pitches uphill at 6.9%. It’s a climb that will suit reigning world TT champion Marlen Reusser to a T but isn’t too long and gruelling for the likes of under-23 rainbow jersey Zoe Backstedt.

The intermediate time check is towards the top but the climb continues at a more gentle incline afterwards, before 6km of fast descent on straight roads into Dijon and a flat finish.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 5: Macon > Belleville-en-Beaujolais (140km, hilly)

There’s no rest on this Tour as immediately after the time trial the peloton heads back into the hills on what should be a great day of action in the general classification. There are a whopping eight categorised climbs encompassing 2,900m of elevation gain on the jagged profile of stage five, all condensed into 140km.

The first five ascents are all in the first 75km, then there’s a brief break of just under 30km before yet more climbing, with the last categorised rise the cat-two Mont Brouilly. It’s 11.5km from the finish and tough enough without all that prior climbing in the legs: the second half features ramps up to 14% and rarely dips below 10%.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 6: Montbrison > Tournon-sur-Rhone (153.4km, hilly)

Stage six continues with the same medium-mountain formula as the race enters the Ardeche and Massif Central, with another six categorised climbs, almost all of them short and punchy barring the biggest test of the day, the category two Col de Lalouvesc. That clocks in at 8.6km averaging 5% and comes 105km into proceedings, straight off the descent of an uncategorised rise, before another long descent to a category three climb 16km from the line and a flat finish.

The Col de Lalouvesc will be key: either a breakaway will make a move stick there, or there will be fireworks in the GC; with Mont Ventoux on the horizon there may well be a pause in hostilities among the big names.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 7: La Voulte-sur-Rhone > Mont Ventoux (146.8km, mountains)

Each year the Tour de France Femmes has visited a legendary climb, from the Col du Tourmalet to the Col de la Madeleine last year, and this year it’s time for the infamous Mont Ventoux to make its debut. There are three other categorised climbs first - the Col de la Grande Limite (6.6km at 5%), Col du Colombier (3.2km at 6.4%), and the Col de Suzette (3.9km at 6.4%) - but today’s action is really entirely condensed into the final 20km.

The Giant of Provence (15.7km at 8.8%) is approached from its toughest side from Bédoin, with a summit finish atop its iconic lunar-like slopes, while if there’s a headwind, as there often is, the 11% final drag will be even more leg-sapping than usual. Expect fireworks.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 8: Sisteron > Nice (171.9km, flat)

After the explosive stage seven stage eight is somewhat calmer, a transitional run towards the coast, albeit not easy by any stretch: it’s the longest stage of the race at over 170km and with another four categorised climbs, encompassing 1,420m of elevation gain in total. After the Col de Routes Aures there’s a very long descent towards the Cote d’Azur - 75km, in fact - with another two short, sharp category four climbs inside the final 15km before a descent onto the Promenade des Anglais and flat finish in Nice.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Stage 9: Nice > Nice (99.2km, mountains)

A processional, champagne-sipping run to the Champs-Elysees this is not: the final stage of the Tour de France Femmes is a punchy one, with a shark’s-tooth profile featuring four laps of the Col d’Eze climb (famous for its inclusion in Paris-Nice). The riders will be climbing and descending all day with no let-up, and there’s every chance the GC standings could be radically overhauled.

The first three ascents are category two, 7.7km at 5.9%, with the last time up shorter but harder, 6km at an average of 7.6% via the Chemin du Vinaigrier, with the descents all the same. The last 2km are flat with the finish line on the Promenade des Anglais.

This could be won by a general classification hopeful, the yellow jersey stamping their authority on the race one last time, or any climber let off the leash on the last day. It should make for a dramatic final day’s racing.

open image in gallery ( ASO )

Who are the contenders?

Chief among the contenders is the Netherlands’ Demi Vollering, who won this race in 2023 and won the Giro d’Italia in June to complete the full set of Grand Tour wins. The European champion is in stunning form, having won Liege-Bastogne-Liege and the Tour of Flanders among other races in a glittering Classics campaign before that recent Giro triumph. Her FDJ Suez-United team is assembled entirely around her, with the likes of French climber Evita Muzic and this year’s Paris-Roubaix champion Franziska Koch excellent lieutenants.

Defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot has had a middling season so far; third place at Paris-Roubaix was the highlight but her results have otherwise been average, including a rather anonymous showing at the Vuelta Femenina. But she has been open about building her season entirely towards the Tour and having cemented her triumph on the Col de la Madeleine last year the inclusion of Mont Ventoux will suit her, although the individual time trial is much better suited to Vollering than the Frenchwoman.

2024 champion Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has been on the podium of every edition and reliably brings her best to the Tour; her Canyon-SRAM squad is a strong one, too, including former Giro d’Italia podium finisher Antonia Niedermaier, who will provide support in the mountains. But although she has been putting in significant time on the TT bike the time trial does not play to her strengths, and she has not looked able to match Vollering on the climbs so far this year.

open image in gallery Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has finished on the podium at every edition of the race, as has Demi Vollering ( AFP/Getty )

Young Spanish prodigy Paula Blasi blew away the field at this year’s Vuelta Femenina and will be co-leader for UAE Team L'IMAD alongside two-time Giro winner Elisa Longo Borghini, with the team able to play multiple cards. Longo Borghini has had a difficult year hampered by illness but is the more natural leader of the team; the squad will likely have to balance the pair’s competing interests, particularly if Blasi arrives in the same barnstorming form as she displayed in Spain, where she was particularly impressive on the toughest climbs - which bodes well for Mont Ventoux. UAE also have Maeva Squiban, who won two stages last year, and Dominika Wlodarczyk, who finished fourth last year.

Movistar leader Marlen Reusser has had a run of bad luck at the sport’s biggest races, including abandoning last year’s Tour with illness on stage one, and crashes and illness have held her back at points this season too. But she won her home race, the Tour de Suisse, earlier this summer and looks to be back at her best; the 34-year-old can climb with the best and as reigning time-trial world champion will expect to gain time on her rivals on stage four.

Finally, SD Worx-Protime will be led by Anna van der Breggen, a legend of the sport who may not be quite at her electric best but is certainly not far off it. Second at the Vuelta and third at the Giro, where she wore the maglia rosa for much of the race, indicate she remains a serious threat. High mountains like Mont Ventoux have always suited her and the ITT also plays in her favour.

News.content:

The FTSE 100 ended a strong week lower on Friday after once again setting a new all-time best, as investors locked in recent gains eyeing rising bond yields.

The FTSE 100 index closed down 29.22 points, 0.3%, at 10,868.05. The blue-chip index had earlier hit a new intra-day high of 10,989.45.

The FTSE 250 ended down 104.12 points, 0.4%, at 23,975.02, while the AIM All-Share closed down 2.35 points, 0.3%, at 762.55.

For the week, the FTSE 100 was up 1.2%, the FTSE 250 was 0.7% and the AIM All-Share was down 1.2%.

Trading got off to a bright start in London on Friday with the blue chip index threatening to surpass the 11,000 milestone but gains evaporated as the day wore on.

NatWest led the risers, up 3.2%, as it raised guidance for 2026 and said it will consider a new share buyback at its annual results, six months earlier than planned, after profit and income beat expectations in the second quarter.

AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould noted this was the fifth time NatWest has beaten consensus forecasts since the Government sold its remaining stake last May.

“The company’s ability to consistently outmatch expectations has undoubtedly been helped by an environment in which interest rates have stayed higher for longer, but the business has also benefited from its own strategic initiatives,” he added.

But IG Group plummeted 14%, the worst FTSE 100 performer, as investors weighed its 1.3 billion dollar acquisition of US fantasy sports and prediction markets operator Underdog.

The deal came as the London-based online trading platform said late on Thursday that total revenue for the first six months of 2026 increased 18% to £642.8 million from £545.2 million a year prior.

Elsewhere, J Sainsbury rose 1.0% as it said it had agreed to sell its Argos business for £120 million, significantly less than it had paid for the company, in order “to fully focus on its core food business”.

The London-based grocer is divesting the brand, which includes its homeware offering, to Swift Partners.

In a research note, JPMorgan analyst Borja Olcese noted Argos has long been an overhang for Sainsbury, and has typically been a driver of the difference between its and peer Tesco’s valuations.

Away from corporate news, investor eyes were on rising bond yields as two Federal Reserve policymakers who dissented from the central bank’s decision to keep interest rates steady earlier this week said that rate hikes were needed now in order to avoid entrenched inflation.

The yield on the US 10-year Treasury stretched to 4.74% on Friday from 4.67% on Thursday. The yield on the US 30-year Treasury widened to 5.27% from 5.21%.

In London, the yield on 10-year gilts jumped to 5.05% from 4.99% at the same time on Thursday.

The Fed held rates at 3.50-3.75% for its fifth straight meeting on Wednesday, with three of the committee’s 12 members dissenting in favour of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike.

“Inflation has been too high for too long,” said one of the dissenters, Beth Hammack, president of the regional Cleveland Fed, in a statement. “The longer that high inflation persists, the more challenging and costly it can be to bring it back down.”

Neel Kashkari, the president of the Minneapolis Fed, who dissented alongside Ms Hammack, said in a statement that he thought it was necessary to “tighten policy incrementally as we gather more data on the path of inflation and employment”.

“If inflation remains elevated, in my view, a potential series of small policy moves would be better than waiting and eventually concluding that even bolder actions were necessary,” he said.

The pound traded at 1.3463 dollars on Friday afternoon, up from 1.3439 at the equities close on Thursday. Against the euro, sterling rose to 1.1702 euro from 1.1671.

John Healey said he will deliver his first budget as Chancellor on October 28, pledging to move “money and power out of Westminster”.

He said the budget would “meet our fiscal rules” and “give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future”.

In European equities on Friday, the CAC 40 in Paris closed up 0.3%, while the DAX 40 in Frankfurt ended up 0.1%.

Stocks in New York were mixed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.2%, while the S&P 500 index and the Nasdaq Composite were flat.

It was another day of diverging fortunes for two of Wall Street’s leading names. Apple was on the back foot after warning that supply constraints and forex headwinds will temper revenue growth in the September quarter, but Amazon surged after strong results.

Apple, which makes the iPhone and iPad, was 9.3% lower after the warning, which came after results which beat expectations. The earnings were the last to be overseen by Chief Executive Tim Cook, who is stepping down in September after 15 years at the helm.

Amazon, meanwhile, soared 13% as it reported “booming” sales at its cloud business, Amazon Web Services.

“AWS is booming, growing 36.7% year-over-year in Q2 – our fastest growth in 18 quarters – and our AI and Chips businesses each eclipsed run rates of more than 25 billion dollars,” said Andy Jassy, chief executive.

“Amazon’s Q2 print was exactly what bulls wanted,” remarked analysts at RBC Capital Markets.

Back in London, Greggs was the worst FTSE 250 performer, falling 7.5%.

RBC cut the baker to ‘sector perform’ from ‘outperform’. It snaps a five-day winning streak for the stock, which included an 18% surge on Wednesday.

Housebuilder Taylor Wimpey fell 4.5%, as it slashed its dividend and lowered its shareholder return policy.

The High Wycombe-based housebuilder now expects annual returns to amount to 4% of net assets, cut from the previous level of around 7.5%. The new target will comprise a minimum of 2% as an ordinary dividend, together with a further 2% returned either via dividends or share buybacks.

The biggest risers on the FTSE 100 were NatWest, up 22.0p at 705.8p, Polar Capital Technology Trust, up 15.0p at 626.5p, Pershing Square Holding, up 88.0p at 3,808.0p, Metlen Energy, up 1.0p at 46.2p and BAE Systems, up 44.0p at 2,094.0p.

The biggest fallers on the FTSE 100 were IG Group, down 246.0p at 1,460.0p, Melrose Industries, down 20.9p at 454.3p, JD Sports, down 3.8p at 89.4p, Experian, down 108.0p at 2,790.0p and Informa, down 28.0p at 885.8p.

Monday’s economic calendar has a slew of manufacturing PMI releases.

Next week’s UK corporate calendar has results from Asia-focused bank HSBC, oil major BP and Guinness owner Diageo.

Football chiefs will consider whether to push for a vote of no confidence on Gianni Infantino following another another day of drastic developments surrounding the embattled Fifa president.

But Infantino’s game-breaking Fifa Forward Enterprise plan is described as “not dead yet”, with the Swiss official still pushing on with his controversial plans after the global governing body issued another round of “clarifications” overnight.

Sources have even spoken of Infantino continuing on in the office as normal. Meanwhile, many outside his decreasingly small circle are highly curious as to what he is “feeling” right now, as a previously invulnerable position has been left so exposed in a matter of days.

open image in gallery FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US president Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Wire )

Above anything, it’s remarkable to think a Fifa president can continue when the most powerful continent have boycotted the World Cup, in Uefa, and two other confederations have at least prepared the ground to follow.

This all in a week that actually started with Infantino berating the media for criticism. One of his most senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro, has also now quit, signing off with a damning statement. That’s just another development that would usually be difficult to survive.

Federation chiefs have already started talking about the process of a vote of no confidence, which would first necessitate a meeting of the Fifa Council and then 43 member associations - a quarter of the 211 - to push for an Extraordinary Congress.

Before that, though, everyone is waiting to see how the dust settles. Football chiefs have even felt it’s all been happening too fast to even properly register.

Amid all of that, Cordeiro’s statement was still clear enough to sum up the main problems with this plan. He wrote of how Fifa “sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt”, ensuring that “selling a permanent stake in football’s most valuable asset to raise $4.2bn makes little sense”.

“Why this deal? Why now?”

The JP Morgan deck for the plan is indeed said to have been “the final straw” for many member associations, including how it seemed to undervalue something as precious as the World Cup - let alone the principle of selling it off. They also pointed to contradictions in how Fifa is now bleating about consultations, but their very documents say terms have been agreed. As one involved figure said, “who agreed them?”

The exclusion of Cordeiro from the process is one of many elements that has only further baffled football.

open image in gallery Cordeiro (left) was a key figure within Fifa as Infantino’s right-hand man ( AFP/Getty )

While the former US Soccer president has been a divisive figure himself, he is seen as one of “the world’s top bankers” given his decades of work at Goldman Sachs.

It would surely have been obvious for Infantino to include him in formulating an idea like this, not least given their proximity. But he didn’t.

Among another key question being asked - of many - is how and why the arbitrary deadline of 19 September was picked.

Sources were wryly laughing at how Fifa’s “clarification” email complained at how their “planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports” only to then plough ahead with this deadline of 19 September. What would have changed if the consultation process hadn’t been “disrupted” by the media?

Sports industry figures have pointed to how a comparable deal between CVC Capital Partners and the Six Nations took two years to go through. Fifa were instead insisting on seven weeks with 211 countries, and that covering a period when most senior federation people are on holiday after a gruelling World Cup.

It is of a piece with so many major decisions under Infantino’s Fifa being rushed through with minimal opportunity for discussion, with the latest apparently the connected expansion of the World Cup to 64 teams.

open image in gallery The pressure is mounting on Fifa president Gianni Infantino ( PA Archive )

If a radical shift like this plan was being taken in normal circumstances, it would come after a strategy department had been suggesting change over a period of time, before going through the board, the finance office and legal.

Except, nothing about this is normal.

The 19 September is otherwise seen by finance figures as a standard attempt to have hard milestones in place before the plan can evolve to formal financial due diligence. It also happens to fit with key Fifa dates, given that there’s an Extraordinary Congress scheduled for 23 November - by which point the presidential nominations are due for the March 2027 election - and the deadline for that agenda is 23 September.

Many figures naturally feel more time is essential, before even considering all the other concerns.

Ultimately, though, there was one major factor putting most voters off.

As a number of sources have said, ‘the association with the Trumps was just never going to fly”.

So much more of the story at least makes sense once it is viewed through the prism of the world around Donald Trump.

Infantino’s long association with a notoriously transactional US president played into a situation where he is suddenly announcing a plan that centrally involves the brother of Trump’s son-in-law - through Josh Kushner’s Thrive Capital - after a year-long plan that very few people apparently knew about.

open image in gallery Josh Kushner is the founder and CEO of Thrive Capital, which has emerged as a proposed lead investor in Infantino’s proposals ( Getty )

That element is said to have infuriated big hitters in the financial community, too. Here was “the most secure, most revenue-generating, most global asset” coming on the market and firms from Silverlake to CVC were not even at the table. That alone could cause awkward discussions at the next round of investor conversations.

And yet it is apparently going to Thrive Capital, which is seen in that sphere as an internet/software venture capital fund.

So, why Kushner?

Many are also seeing Trump’s long flattery of Infantino with a different perspective. As one source puts it, “he talks about him in a way he doesn’t even talk about Benjamin Netanyahu”.

Infantino has had longer and deeper access to the White House than almost anyone outside politics, and stayed close to Trump longer after the type of timescale where relationships with other comparable figures are burned. Look at Elon Musk, for example.

Was it connected to this plan?

The Trump connection could also dictate where this goes next.

As well as a vote of no confidence, federation chiefs have been weighing up potential challengers to be announced in November - from Concacaf’s Victor Montigliani to Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi - but they do still see a path to survival for Infantino.

open image in gallery Gianni Infantino cultivated a relationship with Donald Trump before the staging of the 2026 World Cup ( PA Wire )

If he says he understands the views of the many dissenters and goes in another direction, he could stay.

That direction could even be to still create Fifa Forward Enterprises but without the private equity element, as Uefa have done with Uefa Events SA. The record World Cup profits could then be distributed to member associations at $20m each and everyone moves with a contrite but weakened Infantino.

But will he do that given this connection to the Trumps? What has actually been discussed in the secret negotiations that led to this? Can he unmoor himself from this specific plan in that way, or will he press on and try and get it to a vote?

The next steps could decide more than Infantino’s future.

A New Jersey animal health technology firm is facing allegations of fraud and deceptive business practices following the death of an 11-year-old dog that was misdiagnosed by an artificial intelligence diagnostic tool, a new lawsuit alleges.

Columbia Veterinary Hospital filed the complaint Thursday in Wasco County Court against Zoetis Inc., seeking at least $50,000 in damages.

According to court documents seen by The Oregonian, veterinarians at the hospital in The Dalles, Oregon, used the company’s Vetscan Imagyst system in October 2025 to evaluate tissue samples from an 11-year-old Belgian Tervuren brought in with a rapidly growing neck mass.

Although the AI software identified mast and spindle cell features linked to cancerous tumors, it ultimately categorized the growth as an inflammatory lesion rather than cancer.

Relying on the software’s analysis, staff at the clinic surgically removed the mass. However, a later tissue examination conducted by the Oregon State University Veterinary Diagnostic Lab confirmed the growth was an aggressive form of cancer.

New Jersey animal health technology firm Zoetis Inc. is facing allegations of fraud and deceptive business practices following the death of an 11-year-old dog that was misdiagnosed by an artificial intelligence diagnostic tool, according to a recent lawsuit ( Getty Images )

Because the initial procedure failed to extract all the malignant tissue, the dog was required to undergo a second surgery and later died from post-operative complications, according to the lawsuit.

“The patient’s death resulted directly from the need for a second invasive surgical procedure, particularly within such a short amount of time from the first, which would not have been required if Imagyst had properly identified the tumor as cancerous as Defendant Zoetis represented that it would,” the plaintiffs state in the lawsuit.

The hospital claims it bought the system in 2024 under the impression it delivered expert-level diagnostics.

The filing alleges Zoetis falsely promoted the device as “the world’s most capable veterinary AI analyzer” capable of accurately detecting specific cancers, while omitting known operational limitations.

The suit further alleges that Zoetis modified the initial AI diagnostic report after clinic staff reported the error. Following notification of the misdiagnosis, Zoetis requested a conference call in which company representatives apologized, admitted responsibility and acknowledged that similar errors had occurred with other clients using the Imagyst platform, the complaint states.

The Independent has contacted Zoetis Inc. for comment.

A model village has removed a miniature topless streaker from its football pitch after visitors complained that it was “inappropriate” for a family attraction.

The tiny figure, depicting a woman with exposed breasts running among the football player, was until recently a part of Godshill Model Village on the Isle of Wight.

Its inclusion referenced the 1970s and ‘80s, when streaking at football games was commonplace.

However, the streaker has now been shown the red card by bosses at the attraction following the complaints.

While some visitors expressed their “dismay” at its removal, a director cited concerns that streaking is “very much a feature of a different era”.

Children today would “no longer recognise” the reference, she said.

open image in gallery The streaker, circled in red, on the model village’s football pitch ( Timothy Welstead/Solent News )

Godshill Model Village was established in 1952 and is privately owned by Penny and Stuart Dyer, having passed into their family’s ownership in the 1960s.

It is renowned for its whimsical sense of humour and often incorporates small, tongue-in-cheek details throughout its displays.

Rupert Willoughby, a local and regular visitor to the model village, said he felt “dismay” at the decision to remove the figure, which he said had always brought “innocent delight”.

He questioned whether the character could truly cause offence, suggesting that it was in keeping with the light-hearted spirit of the model village.

However, Ms Dyer, a director of the centre, said the decision followed feedback from a small number of visitors.

open image in gallery The model village is a popular Isle of Wight tourist attraction ( Getty Images )

“The streaker on the football pitch has been part of the model village for many years, and for most visitors has been seen as a light-hearted joke," she said.

“However, we’ve received a small number of comments from visitors who felt it was inappropriate for a family attraction.

“Streaking was very much a feature of a different era.

“It is far less common and is no longer something that younger visitors recognise, so the model has lost much of its original relevance.

“As a business, we listen to customer feedback and after considering the comments, we decided to remove her.

“We appreciate that not everyone will agree with the decision, but our priority is ensuring all visitors feel comfortable and enjoy their visit.”

News.title: Battle rages over access to new ‘miracle’ HIV drug
News.content:
For the first time in the four-decade fight against HIV there is a “miracle” drug that can all but eliminate the risk of infection, but in the Latin American countries where it was tested almost no one can get it.

Trials show that Lenacapavir, made by Gilead Sciences, is almost 100 per cent effective in preventing HIV infection. With just two shots a year, those taking it will avoid contracting the virus even when frequently exposed.

The drug, which many believe could bring an end to the global HIV pandemic, costs $14,000 a dose in the United States. Gilead has agreed to licence generic versions of the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medication at around $60 a dose in 120 low-and middle-income countries, but almost all of Latin America is excluded.

Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Peru are among those with serious HIV epidemics that are shut out, despite having run some of the clinical trials that proved the drug works.

Their status as “upper-middle income countries” means they are too rich to qualify for the cut price generic version and yet they remain too poor to pay the US price.

News.title: Senior dating: a guide to finding love later in life
News.content:
Whether you’re a widow, widower or divorcee, the thought of online dating in later life can feel daunting. However, more and more people are turning to the internet to find romance. Roughly 16 per cent of UK adults are using online dating services to meet a partner, according to Statista. Among them, there are lots of singles over 50 using dating sites.

So here’s how to navigate your senior dating online, with expert advice from psychologist and dating coach Dr Pam Spurr, and sex and relationship coach Angela Vossen.

How do I know if I'm ready to date again as a senior?

Coming out of any relationship is hard. If you’re hoping to date after a divorce, bereavement or break up, it can take a long time to feel ready to date again. Dr Spurr advises taking your time.

“Many people feel bruised, even traumatised, after coming out of a long-term relationship or having been bereaved,” she explains. “Your feelings naturally vary from day to day about whether you're ready to get back out to look for love – or even for fun. A crucial factor is if you've come to the point where you have more good days compared to bad days”.

Dr Spurr explains that good days are the days on which you feel more optimistic about life generally, and you find your thoughts turning to meeting someone new. “That's an important sign that you are healing,” she says. “However, if you're still feeling deeply insecure or are riddled with self-doubt about your worthiness, take your time. When you feel worthy, you will find someone worthy of you”.

Feeling heartbroken? Learn how to get over a break up

How to start senior dating online

If you’re new to online dating, it can feel intimidating at first. The secret is taking things step by step so that you do things at your own pace. The first step, however, should be choosing a senior dating site that will help match you with like-minded people. This will narrow your search and ensure your dating experience is more successful.

Step 1: Create an online profile

Once you’ve decided on a dating site or app and signed up, you’ll be asked to write a dating profile. This should reflect who you are along with your passions, values and what you seek in a partner.

Try to be authentic rather than creating a fantasy version of yourself. If you exaggerate your accomplishments, your date will only feel deceived once they get to know you. Likewise, don’t be tempted to use a photo of yourself from 10 years ago.

What are you waiting for? |  Single and looking to find true love? Sign up today for Telegraph Dating and join more than 220,000 like-minded people. Join today

Step 2: Spark meaningful chats with potential dates

Once you have signed up to a senior dating site and created a profile, you will be free to start looking at other people’s profiles and sending messages to anyone that catches your attention. But how can you initiate a conversation after an introduction?

“When messaging people on dating sites, ask open-ended questions to spark meaningful chats,” says Angela. A good example would be, ‘I can see you enjoy travel. What place have you always wanted to visit but haven’t yet?’ or “tell me more about your love of tennis? Did you watch the US Open?” If things go really well and the chat seems to flow naturally, you may decide to organise a phone chat or ask them out on a date. An initial chat over the phone can help gauge how well you get on and how easily the conversation flows. If this goes well, meeting in person may feel less nerve wracking and a little less ‘blind’.

Step 3: Prioritise your safety

“While most people are well intentioned online, it’s important to protect your safety,” advises Ms Vossen. “Keep personal details private (like where you live or your social media profiles) until you’ve met in person and built trust”. You should also arrange first dates in public places, share your plans with a friend, and trust your instincts if something feels off.

If the first date or two doesn’t quite hit the mark, try not to be too disappointed and remember that you can say no to another date. Ms Vossen says: “Be patient – online dating takes time, but with practice, you’ll gain confidence and enjoy the journey”.

Traditional ways to meet senior singles

Of course, couples continue to meet in a manner that predates online dating sites. If you’re keen to join the older dating scene but find the online world overwhelming, there are plenty of ways to meet people in real life.

1. Holidays and group trips

We are often our best selves on holiday, so it’s the ideal place to find a single senior woman or to meet men if the opportunity presents itself. Why not organise a trip on which you meet new people while doing what you love, whether that’s cycling, walking, sightseeing or just travelling around a new part of the world. There are many escorted tours that cater to specific age groups and interests. They also take away the stress of organising a trip yourself.

“An organised holiday or trip can be a great place to meet someone new and there are many organisations offering these for the over 50s,” says Dr Spur. “A word of caution though, you can spend a lot of money and there's no guarantee that you will meet that special person. However, if it's a place you've wanted to travel to then go with the mindset that you're going to have a great trip. If you meet someone, that's an added bonus”.

2. Activities and social groups

Whether you enjoy walking, reading or volunteering, taking up a new hobby or joining a social group is a great way to enhance your social life and increase your chances of meeting a new romantic interest.

“Joining a club or taking up a hobby can be a fantastic way of meeting singles who enjoy the same pastimes,” says Dr Spur. “You're doing an activity you enjoy knowing that there might also be someone there that will catch your eye”.

If you do meet someone that you’re interested in at a social event, Dr Spur advises starting with a simple ‘hello’ and an easy question such as how long they've been doing that particular activity or hobby. “This can open-up a friendly conversation that might lead to flirting down the line,” she says.

Start online dating for seniors today

Whichever way you decide to start looking for love, approach it in a way that you feel comfortable with. Signing up to an online dating service is a great way to meet other seniors. Remember, it’s never too late to begin a new chapter.
