"I want it [Solheim Cup spot] so badly but sometimes the things you want so badly almost hinder your performance more," Tamburlini, reduced to tears, exclusively told Sky Sports.

"Obviously really disappointed to not be playing the weekend. I really hope I'll still get the spot and I feel like if I do, it'll be a really good motivation for the next couple of events as well.

"Solheim Cup was one of my goals for this year but it's also my first year on the LPGA Tour as well. Trying to establish myself on this tour has been quite difficult this year, so hopefully I get this spot to give myself a bit of a kick.

Image: Tamburlini has dropped to world No 100 after a disappointing campaign

"Not looking great as well with keeping my LPGA card at the moment. Worst case, there's always other options as well. I'm trying to take a little bit of pressure off myself with that. We'll see what happens this weekend on the side of Solheim."

The 26-year-old has finished no higher than 17th on the LPGA Tour this season and has now missed the cut in four of her last six starts, although Tamburlini insists her play is better than her 2026 results show.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tamburlini claimed her maiden Ladies European Tour title at the 2024 Joburg Ladies Open, one of three wins that season

"I feel like honestly over the last seven or eight weeks I've been really close with everybody in my team again," Tamburlini explained. "I feel like we're connecting more again - it was a bit difficult in the beginning of the year, being more in the US.

"I know the scores don't show it, but I feel like my game is so much more solid. I'm starting to recognize my game a lot more again from how it was the last two years really, which is nice - obviously disappointed to not see the results.

"I feel like my game is, as stupid as it sounds, it's not that terrible really. The margins, we all know it, are so small."

Tamburlini was part of Europe's team trip to Bernardus Golf after the Evian Championship earlier this month, but remains hopeful of returning as part of the 12-strong line-up that takes on Team USA from September 11-13.

"They've been all super welcoming as well and open for questions and everything, which has been really nice.

Lottie Woad could move above her in the standings with a top-three finish, while Maja Stark and Carlota Ciganda are among the others who could deny Tamburlini an automatic spot over the coming days.

"I will probably end up looking at the leaderboard [over the weekend] a lot," Tamburlini insisted. "Right now, I'm saying my goal is to not look at it too much!"

Nordqvist will then name her four captain's picks on Monday afternoon, live on Sky Sports. Nanna Koerstz Madsen and Leona Maguire are among the past players in possible contention to be selected, along with former major champion Georgia Hall.

Sports.title: 'Sort yourself out, Harry' - Nasser urges Brook to mature after captaincy snub
Sports.content:
Nasser Hussain has urged Harry Brook to mature after the England white-ball skipper was snubbed for the Test captaincy despite England cricket chief Rob Key confirming the decision was not related to his workload.

Test vice-captain Brook - who oversaw six wins in seven white-ball fixtures against an India side ranked No 1 in the world in July - was overlooked in favour of veteran Joe Root, who undertakes his second spell as Test captain after holding the role between 2017 and 2022.

With the Test team set to embark on a new chapter under incoming head coach Stephen Fleming, former England captain Hussain has rued what he feels is a "missed opportunity" for Brook to take the reins, amid a lack of other suitable candidates.

"I think Harry Brook is a very good captain," Hussain said on the Sky Sports Cricket podcast.

"He's become England's white-ball captain and he's doing it very well.

"But with him are all these off-field antics and that immaturity - you need the mature Harry Brook to come out, and it's been lacking.

"That's why I'm a little bit disappointed in Harry himself, that I think there's a very good captain in there. I think it's a missed opportunity.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brook hit eight stunning sixes after being dropped by India, finishing on 95 not out for England

"One of the things in [new head coach Stephen Fleming's] in-tray will be to sit with Harry Brook and actually say, 'we've had to [give the captaincy] to someone that may not actually want to do it'.

"The lad that will do anything for English cricket in Joe Root is doing it again for English cricket because we couldn't trust you to do the job.

"Sort yourself out, Harry, because I think you should be the next England Test cricket captain."

Key: Brook captaincy snub wasn't related to white-ball workload

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brook reflects on England's ODI series victory over India and what it meant to the team

Key, the managing director of England men's cricket, has confirmed the decision to reappoint Root as Test captain was unrelated to Brook's white-ball workload.

The Test vice-captain - who outgoing skipper Ben Stokes had backed to be his successor - made controversial headlines after being fined £50,000 for an incident involving a nightclub bouncer ahead of an ODI in New Zealand last winter.

"I just don't feel like this is the right time for Harry Brook to be the Test captain," Key told Sky Sports News.

"That was the reason for that decision. I also think it's tough to do all three, but that didn't really come into it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The best of the action from the fourth T20I in Bristol as England demolished India to secure a first-ever series win over their opponents in the format

"We just felt that it was the right time for [Joe Root] and he's the right man.

"Brook's time will come. He's done a brilliant job. He's taken the T20 team to number one in the world. They've just beaten the world champions in 50-over cricket.

"That's a year and a half into a project with him and Brendon McCullum. We've got three formats now where I'm so optimistic about what we can do in all three."

No concerns over Root's return, says Key

Key also backed Root to have a successful second spell at the helm, with England's all-time leading Test run scorer set to lead the team out for a record-extending 66th Test as captain, after deputising for an absent Stokes in the second Test against New Zealand at The Oval.

Root returning to the position had seemed highly unlikely given that, upon stepping down in 2022 after one win from his final 17 Tests as skipper, he revealed his relationship with the role had become "very unhealthy" and cited the "toll" of his years in charge.

"Stephen and I have spoken at length about that and we both feel that Joe Root is by far away the best person to do this job," Key said.

"Last time he did it, I mean I came into this job and it's only then - when you see behind the curtain - do you realise what Joe Root had to put up with.

"His batting was outstanding and I feel I'm so excited to see Joe have the chance to captain the team without all of the distractions."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking after the New Zealand Test win in 2022, Joe Root explained why he had taken the decision to step away from the Test captaincy

Root's batting average dropped from 53.35 to 46.71 during his previous spell in charge, but Key has dispelled any doubts over whether Root has the drive to lead his country once again.

"I think he was really keen when he did it at The Oval. He was relishing that opportunity," said Key.

"He now has a chance to go and show probably just how good a captain he can be.

"Joe Root scores runs and you feel the last time that he did it his game got better and better under the toughest of circumstances.

"No concerns [over a possible drop in form]."

Sports.title: 'Genuine concern' expressed for Saltburn members amid 'Clicky Ponting' scandal
Sports.content:
The North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League has expressed its "genuine concern for the welfare" of Saltburn Cricket Club members as it continues its inquiry into the 'Clicky Ponting' cheating controversy.

Video footage of a Saltburn player, who has been named as Brian Devine, allegedly clicking his fingers to get a caught-behind wicket in a recent second-team game against Norton sparked outrage and went viral on social media.

The NYSDL launched an investigation on Monday, while Saltburn have suspended Devine for the "foreseeable future" and said they were treating allegations of cheating "with the utmost seriousness".

In a further statement, the League said on Friday that it had met with Saltburn officials and had received guidance from the England and Wales Cricket Board to ensure it follows "a due and appropriate process that has to be comprehensive and fair to all".

The League added: "Whilst we understand, to some degree, the interest this issue has generated in the press and media it is imperative that now this process is under way that the rights of all parties are observed, including the overriding principles of natural justice and a right to a fair hearing for any individual or any entity concerned. Anything less risks prejudicing any formal actions which may follow.

"Finally we would want to place on record our genuine concern for the welfare for those at Saltburn Cricket Club and ask for all to take that into account - there are many people at the club and one of our aims will be to provide them with any well-being support we can."

The video footage was met with global condemnation, with the incident making headlines in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and the USA among other countries, while it has been dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' in reference to former Australia captain Ricky Ponting.

Saltburn, 17 points clear at the top of Division Two after winning the match by 159 runs, conceded Wednesday's second-team cup match against Marton in the wake of the controversy.

In response to the video footage on social media, Middlesbrough's second XI captain Rory Cotterill claimed there were two more incidents of cheating in his side's 29-run defeat to Saltburn last month.

Image: Saltburn Cricket Club is at the centre of the sporting scandal

More video footage has since emerged, which allegedly shows Devine, then playing for Pudsey St Lawrence in the Bradford Premier League, repeatedly clicking his fingers while opponents were batting.

Pudsey St Lawrence said in a statement on Thursday: "At no stage was the club aware of any alleged misconduct by Mr Devine, nor were any concerns or complaints raised with the club by opposition teams or umpires who officiated the fixtures in question.

"The club expects its players to uphold the highest standards of integrity and sportsmanship and takes any credible concerns extremely seriously."

The Bradford League added in a statement: "We are aware of the video footage circulating, but it is not our policy to undertake retrospective investigations."

Sports.title: 'It would be a brilliant story' - Key open to Stokes making Ashes return
Sports.content:
England cricket chief Rob Key has left the door open to Ben Stokes coming out of international retirement to play in next summer's home Ashes series against Australia.

Stokes gave up the England Test captaincy and retired from international cricket following his side's 2-1 series defeat to New Zealand in June, which followed a 4-1 Ashes loss to Australia over the winter.

The 35-year-old's decision came after he had been made unavailable for selection for the second Test against New Zealand, after breaching a midnight curfew when out celebrating England's win in the series opener.

There was speculation in the aftermath of the saga that Stokes had been left disappointed by the way he was treated by England's hierarchy, who on Thursday reinstated Joe Root as captain and appointed Stephen Fleming as Brendon McCullum's successor as Test head coach.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stokes reflected on his England career after his final Test match

Asked if the door was still open to Stokes returning to face Australia next summer, England managing director Key told Sky Sports News: "It would be a brilliant story if he does."

Quizzed on whether Stokes had intimated a return, Key said: "No, he hasn't but I wouldn't be surprised. Anything's possible with Ben."

On whether the bridge had been burnt in terms of his own relationship with Stokes, Key added: "No, not at all. Not as far as I'm concerned."

Key: I'm still the right man for the job

Image: Key reasserted his passion to continue leading English cricket after a run of seven defeats in the last nine Tests

Key also reaffirmed his desire to continue in his own position, which has come under scrutiny during a turbulent summer for English Test cricket.

England's managing director has overseen the sacking of a head coach, the retirement of a captain, a plethora of behavioural issues amid allegations of a drinking culture and a run of seven losses in the last nine Test matches.

Asked whether he still had the passion to lead England cricket, Key said: "Yeah, definitely.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from day five of the third Test between England and New Zealand

"I'm optimistic about what we can do.

"The players that are going to take us forward into this next generation are the ones I believe that can go on to become world-class cricketers. There's a couple in there at the moment. There's so many that could go on to become a world-class team

"The key now is to not only have success but sustain it and keep repeating it. That's the system we're trying to put in place.

"In Stephen Fleming and Brendon McCullum, I think we've got the best two coaches"

Fleming's lack of red-ball experience not a concern, says Key

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Key explains why former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming has been selected as head coach of the England Test side

Key also batted away doubts over incoming head coach Fleming's lack of experience with international or red-ball cricket.

Fleming's sole head coaching role since retiring as New Zealand Test captain has been at the helm of the Chennai Super Kings in the IPL, recently vacating the post he has held since 2009 before taking on the England job.

"I think he's [been] one of the most experienced coaches of international cricketers for the last 18 years," said Key.

"You think about that job that he's done in the IPL and you do not forget Test cricket, how to go about it, how to play it with the career that he had as a player, more importantly as a captain as well.

"It's not like for the last 18 years whilst he's been in the IPL he's not been across Test cricket. We've had dealings in the past when our players have gone to Chennai and they've all spoken so highly - I've not met anyone that hasn't spoken highly about Stephen Fleming as a coach.

"I think he's hugely experienced in not only the franchise world, dealing with international cricketers and dealing with Test cricket in particular."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fleming scored an unbeaten 66 in the first innings of the deciding Test as he captained New Zealand to a 2-1 series win in 1999, which saw England fall to last place in the rankings. Can he reverse their fortunes now as Test head coach?

Key also advocated refining an already-established approach to Test cricket, rather than making rash changes to the progress made by the Test team under Stokes and McCullum.

"This is a team now that has lost an entire generation of cricketers bar Joe Root," he said.

"We've had to rebuild the bowling attack. They've lost over a thousand wickets in the last few years and there is so much potential there.

"I believe Stephen Fleming is the best person to get the basics bowlers running and consistently hitting a line and length with all of that potential, all the attributes that they have.

"A refined approach is needed, not a change of approach."

Fleming 'the best possible appointment'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Atherton shares his verdict on Stephen Fleming's appointment as England Test head coach, saying he is the best available choice to lead the side.

Former England captain Michael Atherton says the ECB have made the best possible choice in appointing Fleming, who has a close relationship with white-ball coach McCullum and a proven track record of improving players.

"Fleming was the best appointment the ECB could have made from those available and willing to take the job," Atherton said.

"They spoke to Andy Flower, who said he wasn't interested because of his franchise commitments. I think Fleming is the next best choice.

"They had to find somebody who would work well with McCullum, who remains in charge of the white-ball side. They get on very well and are quite similar in outlook. The players won't be going from one coach who feels completely differently about cricket to McCullum.

"Fleming was a highly regarded captain of New Zealand, he knows the Test game inside out, and he's been a successful coach in franchise cricket with Chennai Super Kings for a long time.

"I don't think it will be radically different to what McCullum was doing, but I think it will be slightly more rigorous, with slightly more attention to detail, and provide a fresh start for a few players.

"It's a different situation to when McCullum was appointed, when England had some top-class players in need of liberation. Now they have younger Test players who need improving, and that is a different job for a coach."

Sports.title: Infantino increasingly embattled after senior adviser resigns over World Cup sell-off plans
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino’s authority has been dealt a fresh blow after Carlos Cordeiro, one of his senior advisers, resigned with immediate effect in protest at proposals to sell a stake in the World Cup.

In the latest embarrassment for Infantino, who saw European FAs threaten to boycott future Fifa tournaments on Thursday, the former US Soccer chief Cordeiro criticised “a bad deal for football” and pointed out that the global governing body already sits on huge amounts of debt-free reserves.

“I cannot stand by while Fifa considers selling a stake in the World Cup,” Cordeiro said in his resignation statement. “I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game.”

Cordeiro has worked for Fifa since 2021 as senior adviser to Infantino. He also operated as a senior adviser to the White House taskforce on this summer’s World Cup.

In resigning he said Fifa “already has the financial capacity to provide [additional financial] support from existing resources”. He added that Fifa would be “mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification” if it sold off a permanent stake.

In addition, Cordeiro questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process. “Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”

Cordeiro’s exit was followed by hefty criticism of Infantino from Fifa’s chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, who told the Associated Press: “It is the project of one person. Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions.”

It adds to the pressure growing on Infantino and Fifa, which is facing calls for an urgent review of its governance after insisting that the planned World Cup sell-off will continue despite the threat of a boycott from all 55 European nations.

View image in fullscreen Carlos Cordeiro with Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino at the White House in 2018. Photograph: Evan Vucci/AP

In a strongly worded statement issued on Friday morning, the Asian Football Confederation backed Uefa’s and Concacaf’s opposition to the creation of a new commercial company, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), saying it “cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward”, and urging Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”.

Fifa had attempted to double down on its position overnight, releasing a statement at 4am UK time saying “we will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA [member association] has the ability to express its vote based on facts,” but it is now clear Infantino is facing united opposition to his proposals from around the globe.

Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC constitute 143 of Fifa’s 211 members, so if their coalition remains united there is no prospect of Infantino getting the votes he needs. The 56-year-old’s position as Fifa president is also under threat for the first time since he was elected in 2016, unless he backs down quickly.

While stopping short of matching Uefa’s boycott the AFC went further than Concacaf in clearly stating that the FFE proposal should be dropped. “The AFC stands in solidarity with Uefa and Concacaf in expressing serious concerns over Fifa’s proposal to introduce private investment into Fifa’s flagship competitions and the decision-making process around FFE,” its statement read. “The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game.

“Football should never have been placed in such a position. Against this backdrop, and in light of the clear positions expressed by Uefa and Concacaf as well as the unprecedented divisions that have emerged across the football world, the AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.

“The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world’s leading football nations. Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered.”

The AFC echoed Uefa and Concacaf’s complaints about a lack of consultation from Fifa, making clear that it is not the first time confederations and the Fifa council have been excluded from major decisions, most notably hosting arrangements for the 2030 and 2034 World Cups.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“The AFC sees this moment as a catalyst for strengthening institutional practices,” the statement continued. “While every Fifa MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote.

“It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.

“The AFC calls upon Fifa to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by Fifa’s statutory bodies.”

View image in fullscreen The hosts for the 2030 World Cup were announced at the Fifa Congress in Zurich in 2024. Photograph: Sergio Pérez/EPA

Fifa had attempted to blame media reporting for the widespread opposition to its scheme, but it is now clear that will not wash with most of its member associations.

“We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation,” a Fifa statement read. “Our planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports. We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

“FFE has been proposed solely to ensure that all Fifa member associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself.

“Nobody is selling football. This is not something Fifa would ever entertain. Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world. Each MA should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future. These are the democratic principles of Fifa.”

If Fifa was to refuse to back down, the first step of the threatened European boycott would come at next month’s Under-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland, with senior Women’s World Cup qualifiers to follow in October.

Sports.title: Fifa rapidly accelerates plan to expand World Cup to 64 teams from 2030 tournament
Sports.content:
Fifa is pushing ahead with plans to expand the World Cup to 64 teams from 2030 and has opened a tender to research companies to assess the economic benefits on a hugely accelerated timescale.

In another twist during a week of astonishing revelations about the global governing body’s plans to reshape football, the Guardian has seen a “research brief” outlining a consultation process to assess the potential increase from the current 48 teams. A period of just four weeks has been allocated for the successful party, which will be selected on 14 August, to analyse the proposed expansion. Fifa has required that the analysis is delivered by 11 September, indicating a decision could be taken this year.

The study will raise further questions about Fifa’s governance just days after Gianni Infantino’s plans to sell off chunks of the World Cup to private investors were revealed. Uefa has already pledged to boycott future tournaments if Fifa does not shelve the scheme and there is likely to be further anger about the proposal to push forward with the 64-team expansion. In another indication of Fifa’s questionable governance it is understood that member associations were not informed about the tender before it was issued.

The invitation to tender explains Fifa is “considering the strategic implications of a possible expansion of the Fifa World Cup beyond the current format”. It asks for an impact assessment regarding tournament revenue and “the change through the eyes of the football ecosystem”. Agencies must submit their proposals for delivering the research by 7 August.

View image in fullscreen Dignitaries including Conmebol’s president, Alejandro Domínguez (second right), at the 2023 press conference to announce some 2030 World Cup games would be played in South America. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP

Infantino said on 12 July that an expansion was “an issue that will be looked at and discussed in the relevant committees after this World Cup”. Speculation had been growing in football’s corridors of power that Infantino would back such a move. It has been pushed by the South American governing body, Conmebol whose president, Alejandro Domínguez, raised the idea again after the 2026 finals had ended.

The 2030 World Cup will be mainly hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain, but individual games are scheduled in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay to honour the tournament’s 100th anniversary. An expansion would make it likely that each of those countries could, as a minimum, host an entire group.

Uefa and Concacaf have been vocal in their opposition to expanding the World Cup further, and Fifa’s decision to push ahead regardless may intensify opposition to the world governing body.

Fifa’s research brief asks for analysis of how different stakeholders might support or resist any expansion, also requesting conclusions about player welfare, product quality and the international calendar. It instructs the relevant agency to identify “the estimated revenue the ticketing, sponsorship and media rights revenues that would be generated in total and specifically by the 64-team format”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Should Fifa confirm a switch to 64 teams, it would mean a short lifespan for the 48-team format, which made its debut this summer. Between 1998 and 2022, 32 teams competed at each World Cup. Eyebrows will be raised about the short time allocated to assess a change of such gravity, which would also have implications for the number of suitable future hosts or regions.

Fifa was approached for comment.

Sports.title: Arsenal target Bruno Guimarães not on Newcastle’s flight to pre-season camp
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimarães was not on Newcastle’s flight to Murcia on Friday lunchtime as Eddie Howe’s former players prepared to meet their new head coach in southern Spain.

As Guimarães, who is believed to be in Brazil, inched closer towards a transfer to Arsenal, Matthias Jaissle was completing his managerial move from Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli. Howe’s successor is expected to arrive at the club’s pre-season training camp in La Manga at some point this weekend.

By the time, shortly after midday, the team’s charter plane took off for the Mediterranean, Newcastle had still to provide formal confirmation of Howe’s departure. It is understood they have been negotiating a financial settlement with their former manager in addition to payoffs for four key members of his backroom staff including the outgoing No 2, Jason Tindall.

Although Howe had told Newcastle of his intention to leave earlier this month, leaks surrounding Jaissle’s imminent appointment caught all parties by surprise. The players learned of Howe’s departure during a day off on Thursday but had the situation fully explained to them by Ross Wilson, the club’s sporting director, at the training ground before heading to Spain.

At the same time, Newcastle’s incoming German head coach was understood to be finalising a four-year contract at St James’ Park after an £8m compensation package was agreed with Al-Ahli. Jaissle is already in Europe after remaining in Portugal rather than returning to Jeddah with his squad following the conclusion of a pre-season training camp on the Algarve on Wednesday.

The 38-year-old former RB Salzburg manager is assembling his own backroom staff and now has only three weeks before his first Premier League season begins with a home game against Liverpool.

One of his first tasks will be to hold talks with Guimarães about the Brazil midfielder’s future. Guimarães – who was close to Howe – is booked on a flight to Spain on Sunday but there are suggestions he could board a London-bound plane instead should Arsenal offer around £75m.

View image in fullscreen Joelinton could be on his way to the Saudi Arabia league this summer. Photograph: Siu Wu/EPA

Although Manchester United are exploring a move for Lewis Hall, Jaissle has reason to be more confident of keeping the influential left-back. Newcastle are said to be determined to retain one of their best young players but could be more receptive to any bid from Saudi Arabia for Joelinton. Guimarães’s compatriot is believed to be keen on a move to the Middle East.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

While Besiktas covet another Newcastle midfielder in Joe Willock, Wilson appears close to securing a new goalkeeper. A £26m deal for the Braga and Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek is expected to be completed over the weekend.

Should that move for the 24-year-old progress as planned, Nick Pope, Newcastle’s first-choice, will almost certainly become yet another departure in a turbulent summer on Tyneside.

Sports.title: Chelsea fined £10m and given suspended transfer ban by FA over agent breaches
Sports.content:
Chelsea have been fined £10m by the FA and served with a suspended transfer ban for multiple violations of transfer rules during the Roman Abramovich era.

The sanction reflects a similar punishment handed to the Blues by the Premier League earlier this year after the club was found to have used unlicensed agents and sought to obscure the nature of their transfer dealings between 2009 and 2022. Deals involving Chelsea legends Samuel Eto’o, Eden Hazard and Willian were among those found to have breached the rules. The commission originally handed down a stronger sanction that would have given Chelsea a suspended six-point deduction, but it was overturned after an appeal by the club.

The offences were self-reported by Chelsea when new ownership entered Stamford Bridge in 2022 and the disciplinary panel praised the club for its actions as well as its co-operation through the hearing. Chelsea, who are also operating under a settlement agreement with Uefa, said they had “worked openly and transparently with all regulators” and were “pleased to confirm that this brings all regulatory proceedings against the club to a close”.

Written reasons published by the FA show the independent commission took a very dim view of the Abramovich-era administration, saying their rule-breaking showed “a shameful and arrogant disregard for the rules of the game … which has done so much to bring the game of football in general, and the name of CFC into disrepute”. They also said, however, that there were aspects of the case brought by the FA that caused them “particular concern”.

While praising the FA’s co-operation on the case, the commission criticised the governing body for both failing to charge individuals related to the misdemeanours and for requesting that a sporting sanction should not be applied as punishment. After a submission by the Premier League, which also argued against a sporting sanction, Chelsea appealed against the commission’s original sanction and the six-point deduction was replaced with a suspended two-window ban on registering new players. While the commission had originally argued Chelsea had both sought and gained a sporting advantage from their actions, the appeal board found that there was insufficient evidence to show that any advantage had actually been achieved.

The Premier League and the FA had been examining tens of millions of pounds in secret payments made by offshore companies that were owned by Abramovich. Details of the transactions were uncovered as part of Cyprus Confidential, an investigation by the Guardian and international media partners, based on a leak of data from Cypriot financial services firms that the Russian oligarch used to manage his vast fortunes.

Deals revealed by the leak included apparent off-book payments to Hazard’s agent and an associate of the title-winning manager Antonio Conte.

Sports.title: Franco Baresi was not only the captain but the moral heart of great Milan team
Sports.content:
There are very few players who become bywords for their position, who enjoy universal acclaim. But for anybody who watched football in the late 80s or early 90s, Franco Baresi was the central defender. He was unsurpassed, obviously the best in his position in the world, the definition of the art of the defending. The oddity is, he really wasn’t like very many other defenders at all.

Baresi had just turned 19 when he won his first scudetto at Milan under Nils Liedholm. It was 1979 and Italian football was still dominated by the ideals of catenaccio. Most defences comprised a libero, two man-markers and, if you were lucky, an attacking left-back. But not Liedholm’s. The Swede was a pioneer in Serie A of zonal marking, and the idea that the game was not a series of physical battles but a question of space. Baresi was only 5ft 9in and a teenager. More traditional coaches might not have trusted him. But Liedholm saw an impeccable reader of the game, even at that age. Baresi was an ever-present, not only in the league but in the Coppa Italia and Uefa Cup as well.

That turned out to be a traumatic season for the club, with players arrested on the pitch after the final game of the season as part of the Totonero betting scandal, for which Milan were ultimately relegated. With the club in financial chaos, promotion was followed by another relegation and, although they were promoted again, the future seemed bleak before Silvio Berlusconi took over in 1986. Baresi remained loyal throughout. His parents died before he turned 16 and Milan became a sort of surrogate family.

He never played for any other club, amassing 719 appearances in all competitions over 20 years. And yet, he could easily have been an Inter player. Baresi’s brother Giuseppe, two years his elder, was already at Inter when Franco was offered a trial at the age of 14. Inter wondered if he was big enough to make it and asked him to come back the following year. So Franco went for a trial at Milan – which he insisted had always been his club – and was taken on.

Berlusconi was an outsider, determined to disrupt the establishment. In Arrigo Sacchi, who was appointed in 1987, he found a coach in the same vein: a radical who followed Liedholm’s tentative steps into the world of zonal marking with a giant leap into a full-blown flat back four and hard pressing. In the Serie A of the age it was almost unthinkably revolutionary. Conservatives were sceptical and, when Milan lost their second game of the season 2-0 at home to Fiorentina, and followed that up with defeat to Espanyol in the Uefa Cup and a disappointing draw against Cesena, the joke was that Berlusconi’s new messiah would not make All Saints’ Day, which is 1 November.

Form began to turn around, but Sacchi worried he had pushed the players too hard and eased back on training, at which point Baresi made a decisive intervention. He begged Sacchi to push the players even harder. It was vital, he said, that the players didn’t forget, that they came to learn the new way of playing, of working out their position not according to preset formulas but through constantly evolving reference to opponents, their teammates, the ball and the space, to internalise the processes until they became instinctive.

View image in fullscreen Franco Baresi (kneeling, second left) and his Milan teammates celebrate beating Steaua Bucharest 4-0 to win the 1989 European Cup, for many the high point of their football under Arrigo Sacchi. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

For Sacchi, it was a huge moment. Baresi was not only the captain, but the moral heart of the team. If he was on board with the revolution, Sacchi realised, the squad would follow. Milan, with their ultra-modern style, won the scudetto in 1988 and backed it up with consecutive European Cup wins, playing some of the most memorable football ever witnessed. Baresi was central to it, not only snuffing out opposing forwards but constantly analysing and organising, and also initiating counterattacks. The clipped forward pass became a trademark, but his greatest skill was his pass selection. He just didn’t give the ball away.

His inspirations were creative players plus Ruud Krol, but Baresi was also tough. Gianfranco Zola called him the best defender he ever played against but observed that afterwards “your feet need loads of ice and anti‑inflammatories”. Baresi dished it out, as defenders in Serie A in those days had to, but he could also take it. He played more than an hour of a Milan derby in 1989 with a broken arm, helping keep a clean sheet, and, at the 1994 World Cup, managed to recover from knee surgery required after tearing his cartilage in the second group game in time to play in the final. Again, he oversaw a clean sheet but, cruelly, failed from the spot in the shootout as Italy lost to Brazil.

View image in fullscreen A Milan fan lays flowers next to a shirt of former captain Franco Baresi at Casa Milan. Photograph: Daniele Mascolo/Reuters

International football never quite gave Baresi the highs the club game did. He was part of the World Cup-winning squad in 1982 but didn’t play a minute, and was part of squads that got to the last four of Euro 88 and Italia 90, but he never achieved the same glory with Italy that he did with Milan.

And so the memory of him will always be in the red-and-black shirt, anticipating the game, stepping implacably in front of an opponent, shrugging him off and clipping a perfectly weighted ball in to a forward’s feet, the defining image of Italy’s new era of defending.

Sports.title: Who should win the men’s Ballon d’Or?
Sports.content:
Harry Kane

Seventy-three goals in 64 games for club and country – the second most prolific season by any player in history after Lionel Messi’s 82-goal campaign in 2011-12 – not bad for a man who once sat on the bench alongside Jamie Vardy in the Championship. Harry Kane was not a teenage prodigy like a few of the other players on this list but here he is crashing football’s top table at the age of 33.

It feels strange that a player who has scored at least 24 goals in each of the last 12 seasons, has won back-to-back Golden Boots in the Premier League, a World Cup Golden Boot and two European Golden Shoes, has never finished higher than 10th in Ballon d’Or voting.

The numbers were always there but now he is adding the silverware. Kane’s trophy drought ended when Bayern Munich won the Bundesliga last year and that triumph has opened the floodgates. Another Bundesliga title followed this season, alongside the DFB-Pokal and German Supercup.

England did not end their trophy drought at the World Cup but their captain scored six goals and overtook Gary Lineker as England’s top scorer at the tournament, ensuring he remained in contention for the Ballon d’Or.

Lamine Yamal

“It’s about being calm. When I’m in the area with the ball, I decide what happens,” said Lamine Yamal in February after he had scored the first hat-trick of his career in Barcelona’s 4-1 win against Villarreal. For most 19-year-olds this would sound like arrogance, but Yamal is not like most 19-year-olds.

He offered more proof of that this summer. The Spain forward became the first player to appear in a European Championship final and a World Cup final before turning 20 – and he won both. He only scored one goal at the World Cup, which was a modest return by his own lofty standards, but he was influential throughout. He won a gamechanging penalty in the semi-final against France, he made more successful take-ons than Messi across the tournament, and he had a hand in breaking down an Argentina side hellbent on baiting him into a physical duel in the final. He achieved all this after going into the tournament with a hamstring injury. Joe Hart captured the mood best after the final, saying: “Lamine Yamal is 19 years old. What a beautiful day for him. He’s 19 and has completed football.”

Add in the 24 goals and 18 assists he racked up in 45 appearances for Barcelona as they won La Liga and the Supercopa, and he has a strong case to go one better than his runners-up finish in last year’s Ballon d’Or.

Rodri

“We’ll see the real Rodri at the World Cup,” said Pep Guardiola last October, when the Manchester City captain returned to action after suffering an ACL injury. There were doubts that the 2023 Ballon d’Or winner would ever return to his best. But, as with most things in football, Guardiola was right.

Rodri was the heartbeat and the safety blanket in the Spain team, dictating every phase of the game, controlling possession and extinguishing almost every danger posed to his backline – Spain only conceded one goal in their eight matches at the tournament. Rodri completed 756 passes (more than anyone at the tournament) and he also topped the charts for touches, line-breaking passes and passes in the opposition third. In the final alone he completed 101 passes, completely strangling the life out of Argentina to the extent that they did not have a single shot on target.

He lifted the trophy as Spain’s captain, won the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player and earned a place in one of football’s most exclusive clubs as only the fourth man in history to have won the World Cup, European Championship, European Cup and Ballon d’Or, joining Gerd Müller, Franz Beckenbauer and Zinedine Zidane.

Kylian Mbappé

Kylian Mbappé went toe-to-toe with his old Paris Saint-Germain teammate Lionel Messi at the World Cup. They battled it out for the trophy, the Golden Boot, the Golden Ball and a place in the history books as the competition’s all-time leading scorer. He won two of the four. His two goals in the third-place playoff against England ensured he became the first man to win the Golden Boot twice. It also brought him to 22 goals in World Cups – one more than Messi – and made him the first man to reach double figures in a single edition since Müller in 1970.

And yet, it was not what Mbappé wanted. “I would have preferred not to be the top scorer and to have played in the final,” said the France captain. His domestic season was also prolific but disappointing, bringing goals and individual glory but no silverware. He scored 42 goals in 44 appearances, finishing the season as the top scorer in La Liga and the Champions League, but he did not win either trophy. The goals flowed but the medals did not follow. As Kane has discovered, goals alone are rarely enough to win the Ballon d’Or.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé has scored 22 goals in 22 matches at World Cups. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

Lionel Messi

Lionel Messi sat on the floor alone in a stadium of 80,000 people, boots off, staring into the distance as Spain’s substitutes streamed past him in celebration. It was not the fairytale image the Argentina captain had envisioned as he left the world stage. And, given his performances over the previous six weeks, it felt as if he deserved better even if his team did not.

Some expected Messi’s tournament to be a nostalgia act – a former great wheeled out for one last World Cup as he prepares for his 40th birthday. But then he went and scored a hat-trick in Argentina’s first game. He scored twice against Austria, then added another against Jordan. He stamped his authority on the tournament in the group stage and proceeded to drag Argentina through the knockouts: a goal against Cape Verde, a goal and an assist against Egypt, an assist against Switzerland, and two more assists to sink England in the semi-final. Had it not been for Mbappé’s brace in a bizarre third-place playoff, he would have collected the Golden Boot.

Could he win the Ballon d’Or having lost the World Cup final? In only four of the last 19 years has the award gone to a player who did not win the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa América in the same year. But three of them were won by Messi. A ninth Ballon d’Or is unlikely but the fact he is in this conversation at all – at 39 while playing in MLS having lost a final – is testament to his greatness.

This is an article by WhoScored

Sports.title: Jaissle heads for Newcastle after success in Saudi Arabia that has eluded so many
Sports.content:
Taking over a big, underachieving port city club with a loyal fanbase that is desperate for success should not faze Matthias Jaissle. Should he take the role vacated by Eddie Howe, the 38-year-old German will leave Jeddah as a hero and arrive in the north-east as one of the most successful coaches in the history of Asian football.

A decade younger than Howe, Jaissle has achieved plenty, not only surviving in a Saudi Pro League that chews through coaches at a rapid rate but emerging victorious. It also helps that Al-Ahli and Newcastle share the same Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) owners.

Newcastle fans may know little about the former centre-back, whose playing career was cut short by injury, but that was also the case in Saudi Arabia when he arrived three years ago. Austria’s Bundesliga is not followed much in Asia, so two titles won with Red Bull Salzburg did not mean a great deal: neither did Jaissle’s association with Ralf Rangnick.

Fans were more focused on Al-Ahli’s recent return to the top flight, after a first season in the second tier, and were contemplating an influx of big-name players. A little different to the situation at St James’ Park with stars such as Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon already gone and others seemingly about to follow.

In Jeddah, Riyad Mahrez, Roberto Firmino, Édouard Mendy, Franck Kessié and others arrived in a summer when the club was acquired by PIF. For a team that had been in the doldrums a year earlier, it was quite a turnaround.

Despite all that Al-Ahli may have been the perfect club for Jaissle. The fans are famously passionate but had only one domestic league win since 1984. In Asia there had been two comprehensive Champions League final defeats. Compared to Al-Hilal, Al-Nassr and Al-Ittihad – also in the PIF stable – the Green corner of Jeddah had been relatively starved of success and, for a while, challenging again was enough.

For the then 35-year-old, dealing with such names did not seem a problem. His straight-talking style, with the foreign stars treated the same as the locals, drew a positive response. With his wealth of attacking talent Jaissle tried to win possession as high as possible to give players such as Mahrez the chance to shine. His preferred attack-minded, high-intensity playing style may move up a gear by the North Sea compared to the heat and humidity of the Red Sea.

View image in fullscreen Galeno (right) was a key signing for Al-Ahli under Jaissle and brought the best out of Ivan Toney in attack. Photograph: Reuters

In his first season Al-Ahli finished third, 11 points ahead of their fierce local rivals Al-Ittihad and, crucially, qualified for the AFC Champions League Elite. The second season was more difficult, for a while at least. After the departure of Allan Saint-Maximin, Jaissle wanted a replacement winger but, instead, Ivan Toney was signed and the England striker started slowly. Results dipped but were improving by January 2025 when the axe threatened to fall. Max Allegri was ready to take over, the kind of eye-catching coach that fans often want. But not in this case – members of the Green Army supported Jaissle, who had always taken time out to praise and talk to fans. A group of them appeared at the training ground with banners telling club management they should be the ones to go.

And it worked. Al-Ahli said Jaissle was staying with their full support. In came a winger, Galeno from Porto, and with the Brazilian getting the best out of Toney, Al-Ahli moved up a gear. They finished fifth in Jaissle’s second season but got more points. It was all about the Champions League, however. In the semi-finals, they defeated Al-Hilal, 19-time Saudi and four-time Asian winners. Then, in May 2025, in front of 60,000 fans in Jeddah, Kawasaki Frontale of Japan were defeated.

Then Al-Ahli did it again, winning the Asian title for a second time last May to become the first team since their Jeddah rivals, Al-Ittihad (in 2004 and 2005), to clinch successive Champions League crowns.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They also had a title challenge at home that only faded in the final weeks with Toney scoring 32 goals. In 34 games the team collected 81 points, 14 more than the previous season, and had Al-Nassr and Al-Hilal not been so consistent then it could have been a spectacular double.

The focus for the new season, due to start in August, was all about the Saudi Pro League title; but that should be someone else’s concern now.

Jaissle was recently linked with Al-Hilal and while that wouldn’t have gone down well with fans in Jeddah, he heads to Newcastle with the blessing of most. The German was always likely to return to Europe, and departs with success in Saudi Arabia, having won major titles. Many more experienced coaches have failed in that regard. Newcastle will be a different and tougher challenge.

He is not part of the elite any more but taking Newcastle closer to the Premier League’s top four would be a good start.

Sports.title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches
Sports.content:
The FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.

The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.

Across the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.

Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.

“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.

Sports.title: Arsenal reach £77m agreement in principle to sign Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle - as Premier League champions plan medical next week
Sports.content:
Arsenal reach £77m agreement in principle to sign Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle - as Premier League champions plan medical next week

Arsenal have reached an agreement in principle to sign Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle - and have set aside a day next week for the Brazil midfielder's medical.

It is understood that the fee agreed for the Newcastle captain is £77million plus add-ons.

The 28-year-old's contract has not yet been signed and finer details are to be sorted but Daily Mail Sport can confirm a deal is now very close.

The Magpies had been reluctant to part with their captain after losing other key players - such as Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon - this summer but the Premier League champions have gone all out to get the deal done.

Bruno Guimaraes is set to become the latest key Newcastle player to leave this summer

The Brazilian was part of the Newcastle side that won the club's first major trophy for 70 years - the Carabao Cup in March 2025

He is the third key player to leave Newcastle this summer, joining Anthony Gordon (second left) and Sandro Tonali (second right), while manager Eddie Howe has also left the club

As revealed by Daily Mail Sport, Guimaraes dropped a bombshell on the Newcastle hierarchy several weeks ago by informing them of his desire to leave. And he did not fly with the rest of the Toon squad to their pre-season training camp in La Manga on Friday.

The Magpies also saw manager Eddie Howe leave the club yesterday after four and a half years.

He would become Arsenal's fourth signing of the summer, after they made Piero Hincapie's loan deal from Bayer Leverkusen permanent, signed free agent former Leeds United goalkeeper Illan Meslier and struck a £36m deal for Club Brugge's Greece winger Christos Tzolis.

Arsenal first tried to sign Guimaraes in 2022 from Lyon, but Newcastle stole a march on the midfielder, who has won 48 caps for his country and played in this summer's World Cup.

Sports.title: Eddie Howe sends emotional message to Newcastle fans as club confirms bombshell exit - and labels his five-year spell at St James' Park a 'privilege of my lifetime'
Sports.content:
Eddie Howe sends emotional message to Newcastle fans as club confirms bombshell exit - and labels his five-year spell at St James' Park a 'privilege of my lifetime'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Eddie Howe has delivered an emotional farewell to Newcastle United supporters as the club confirmed his departure in a statement on Friday.

Howe, who established Newcastle as European regulars and won the 2025 Carabao Cup during his near five-year spell in charge at St James' Park, came to an agreement to leave his role with immediate effect this week after contemplating his future over the summer.

The Englishman informed Newcastle of his wish to leave earlier this month but agreed to stay on until a replacement was found, with German coach Matthias Jaissle now stepping in to succeed him ahead of the new 2026-27 season.

As part of a statement shared by the club to their website on Friday, Howe described the opportunity as a 'privilege of a lifetime'.

'After a period of personal reflection, I have decided that now is the right time for me to step away from my role as head coach of Newcastle United,' he confirmed.

'After nearly five years of giving my life, heart and soul into the club with unrelenting energy, I feel that it is in the best interests of both myself and the club to step away, recharge and take a break.

Eddie Howe delivered an emotional farewell statement to Newcastle United fans on Friday

'Although it's been incredibly difficult to make this decision, I know in my heart that it's the right one. I have always put the best interests of Newcastle before my own in every single decision I have made whilst I've been here and this one is no different.

'It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have been the manager of Newcastle United.

'It is difficult to put into words what this club, the city and its supporters mean, and will always mean, to me and my family. From the moment myself, Jason and all of the staff arrived nearly half a decade ago, Newcastle instantly felt like home and the people here welcomed us with open arms. We took huge pride in representing the club from day one and this city will always hold a very special place in our hearts.

'There have been so many incredible moments in our time here. From fighting relegation in our first season to the numerous unforgettable nights at St. James' Park in the Champions League soon after. The progression was fast.

'Everyone came together, united and what a force we became, culminating in bringing home our first domestic trophy in 70 years. These are all memories that I will cherish for the rest of my life.

'I would like to put on record my sincere thanks and appreciation to Yasir Al-Rumayyan, Jamie Reuben, Jacobo Solís and everyone at PIF, David Hopkinson, Ross Wilson and the entire ownership and leadership group for placing their trust in me and for giving me the opportunity to lead this special football club.

'I remain incredibly positive and enthusiastic about the future of Newcastle. The club is in fantastic hands with a great leadership team and I have no doubt together, alongside whoever comes in to replace me, they will continue to deliver success on the pitch.

'Thank you to Jason Tindall, Graeme Jones, Stephen Purches, Simon Weatherstone, Dan Hodges, Andy Howe and Jordan Tribe for their incredible loyalty, support and dedication and to all of the amazing staff behind the scenes whose hard work and loyalty makes this club what it is.

Howe steered Newcastle to Carabao Cup glory in 2025, ending their 70-year trophy drought

'A special thank you to all of the players who have represented the club during my time here. Without you, nothing would have been possible and it's been an honour to have coached you all.

'Finally, and most importantly, thank you to our incredible supporters. Your passion and loyalty have inspired me every single day. To stand on the touchline at St. James' Park as your manager with the honour of representing your club has meant more to me than you will ever know.

'While my journey as manager has now come to an end, the affinity and love I will always hold for Newcastle United never will.

'Thank you for everything. I wish the club every success for the future.'

The timing of Howe's departure has rocked Tyneside, even though it has not come as a surprise on the back of a turbulent 12 months.

After losing star striker Alexander Isak last September, England winger Anthony Gordon and Italy midfielder Sandro Tonali have been sold to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively this summer.

Arsenal have also today reached an agreement in principle to sign midfield leader Bruno Guimaraes for a fee that is understood to be worth £77million plus add-ons.

As revealed by Daily Mail Sport, Guimaraes dropped a bombshell on the Newcastle hierarchy several weeks ago by informing them of his desire to leave. And he did not fly with the rest of the Toon squad to their pre-season training camp in La Manga on Friday.

After arriving at St James' Park in November 2021, Howe accelerated Newcastle's status as a Premier League club by steering them to Champions League qualification on two occasions and ending their 70-year drought for a major domestic trophy.

David Hopkinson, Newcastle United's CEO, added: 'Eddie and his staff leave with the deep gratitude and respect of everyone at Newcastle United, and with a lasting place in the club's history.

Howe is being replaced by German coach Matthias Jaissle, who leaves Al-Ahli in Saudi Arabia

'While we are naturally disappointed to see Eddie leave, we remain immensely thankful for everything he has done for the club.

'On behalf of our owners, Board, players, staff and supporters, I would like to extend sincere thanks to Eddie for his outstanding service and leadership, and wish him and his family every success and happiness for the future.'

Sports.title: David Moyes makes call over Celtic star, Inter Milan continue pursuit of £30m-rated Liverpool man, Bournemouth agree deal for Benfica defender - and West Ham step up chase for midfielder Arne Engels: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
David Moyes makes call over Celtic star, Inter Milan continue pursuit of £30m-rated Liverpool man, Bournemouth agree deal for Benfica defender - and West Ham step up chase for midfielder Arne Engels: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Arsenal closing in on Bruno

Arsenal have reached an agreement in principle to sign Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle - and have set aside a day next week for the Brazil midfielder's medical.

It is understood that the fee agreed for the Newcastle captain is £77million plus add-ons.

For the full story click HERE

ISAAN KHAN

Szmodics back in at Derby

Derby County are re-signing forward Sammie Szmodics from Ipswich Town on a season loan with an obligation to buy worth £5.4million. He was on loan at Derby in the second half of last season.

Szmodics signed for Ipswich from Blackburn for £9m in 2024 on a four-year deal.

Stoke City are among the clubs keen on Ipswich striker George Hirst.

Sammie Szmodics scored four goals in the Premier League for Ipswich in 2024-25

Moyes makes call as Everton pursue Celtic's Johnston

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill has confirmed Everton have made contact over their interest in right-back Alistair Johnston.

O'Neill said Everton boss David Moyes had called him to warn him the approach was coming.

'Everton have been in contact. I'm not sure whether there has been a bid in for that one.

'In fairness, David [Moyes] did call me last weekend to tell me that there would be contact.

'But I don't know how far that has progressed, or if it has at all.'

Everton say Canada international Johnston, 27, is one of a number of options they are considering.

United keeping tabs on Hall

Manchester United remain appreciative of Newcastle left back Lewis Hall but acknowledge it would be a difficult transfer to pull off.

The club are still assessing market movements, checking who is available at the right price, before deciding on their next priority position. Another midfielder has been at the forefront of their thinking while another forward still hinges on Marcus Rashford departing. Despite interest from other clubs, as it stands, he remains likely to start the season at United.

Cover at left back is required as United are going into the new season with Luke Shaw, who has one year left on contract, as their only senior option in that position. Harry Amass can cover but has been told he would be better seeking first team opportunities elsewhere.

Manchester United are keen on Newcastle left back Lewis Hall

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise once Matthias Jaissle is in place.

Though midfielder Bruno Guimaraes may yet join Arsenal, if they make a formal offer over £80m, the club want to add players to ensure they are competitive.

Hamer heading back to Coventry

Coventry are closing on a deal to bring back midfielder Gustavo Hamer from Sheffield United. The 29-year-old Brazilian has one year left on his deal.

He spent three years at Coventry after joining from PEC Zwolle, before moving to Sheffield United in August 2023.

Inter continue Jones pursuit

Inter Milan are continuing to pursue Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones but have still to hit the Anfield club's valuation.

The 25-year-old has cut a frustrated figure in recent months and has wanted more regular game time.

He has one year left on contract and Liverpool say they are relaxed about his situation.

Liverpool value the academy graduate around £30million but Inter's last offer was just under £22m.

The Italian club were interested in January and proposed a loan with a view to a permanent move but that was also turned down by Liverpool.

Inter Milan are continuing to chase Curtis Jones but are yet to meet Liverpool's valuation

Piero Ausilio, Inter's sporting director, confirmed he was still on their radar earlier this summer, saying: 'Curtis Jones - we are paying attention to him. We didn't hide. We understand what the developments will be.'

Teammate Federico Chiesa, another who could depart, also told Italian media that Jones asked him what it is like to live in Italy.

The midfielder has been with Liverpool since he was nine and signed his first professional contract with them in 2018.

Inter yesterday confirmed the signing of England defender John Stones on a free transfer.

Cherries swoop for Silva

Bournemouth have agreed their £25m deal with Benfica to sign defender Antonio Silva.

The 22-year-old centre back captained and played 90 minutes for Benfica in their emphatic 5-0 Europa League qualifying win against St Gallen last night.

The transfer is worth £21.4million plus £4.3m in add-ons.

The Portugal international is due to travel over this weekend to have a medical and complete his move.

Antonio Silva is set to move to Bournemouth from Benfica

Leicester bring in Championship forward

Leicester City have signed Swansea City forward Liam Cullen for an undisclosed fee.

The Wales international, who has agreed a three year deal, can play as a centre-forward, attacking midfielder or right winger.

He previously worked under manager Russell Martin at Swansea.

Cullen, 27, said: 'When this opportunity came about and with the size of the club and the project they’re getting started with now, I thought it was the perfect fit for me.'

Welsh forward Liam Cullen has signed for Leicester, who will play in League One this season

Hammers trying to nail down Engels

West Ham are moving ahead on talks for Celtic midfielder Arne Engels.

The 22-year-old was the subject of bids up to £25million from Nottingham Forest in January which Celtic rejected.
