World.title: Over 1,000 students later, Richmond, B.C., man still teaching English for free as feds cut lessons
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twice a week, the party room of the Mino Club Cafe in Richmond, B.C., is converted into a classroom.

Normally, the café doubles as a children's play space and restaurant. But on Tuesdays and Saturdays, it also becomes a place to learn.

Inside, dozens of people, mostly newcomers to Canada, work hard at one thing.

"I come here want to improve my English," said Meice Xu, an immigrant from Shanghai.

It all happens under the watchful eye of Masih Sabet, who has taught over 1,000 students for free in Richmond since 2017.

Meice Xu, one of the students in Masih Sabet's Richmond English class, explains what she's been learning. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

"We call it [the] English Friendship Corner," said Sabet. “We help them to create friendship between themselves. And they learn that they are not alone in this.”

His lessons have been a vital service amid ongoing federal cuts to English class funding for new permanent residents and refugees.

This September, Ottawa will stop funding intermediate English training altogether.

SUCCESS, a B.C.-based non-profit that helps immigrants, said it has had to close two language centres in Richmond since last year.

"We'll have to reduce the size for the upcoming year as well," said Queenie Choo, CEO of the organization.

WATCH | Masih Sabet teaches English in a café turned classroom: This volunteer is teaching newcomers English for free amid federal cuts to language programs | Duration 2:36 A volunteer in Richmond has taught over 1,000 new immigrants English, all for free. This comes at a time when the federal government is slashing English programs for newcomers, with a new round of cuts coming in September. The CBC’s Steven Chua reports.

The federal class, called Language Instruction for Newcomers to Canada, has been helping people integrate into Canadian society since 1992.

It comes in two distinct packages: Stage 1 focuses on beginner-level English to get people functioning at a basic level in Canadian society, while Stage 2 is intermediate, and often needed for people pursuing white collar work.

Both of these have been strained by funding reductions.

But in September, it’s Stage 2 classes that will be losing all their funding from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).

$234M cut to settlement service

From 2024 to 2027, the federal government anticipates slashing $234 million in overall settlement service provider funding.

This is money given to places like SUCCESS that help new immigrants integrate into Canada. It generally includes cash earmarked for information, employment and language services.

The IRCC said funding is tied to the number of permanent residents coming to Canada, and that it's stopping Stage 2 English funding to prioritize basic language training.

Major immigration cuts began in 2024 when the federal government announced it would reduce the number of new permanent residents by more than 200,000.

During the first quarter of this year, Statistics Canada reported a 20 per cent drop in permanent immigrants compared with the same time last year.

Lessons offer a sense of community

Those working with newcomers say a lack of access to English classes can have consequences.

"There’s a delay in kind of the integration, delay in finding a job or delay in even the overall economic integration into the community," Choo said.

Masih Sabet says his lessons aren't just about teaching English, but about giving people a community gathering space too. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

Sabet, an immigrant himself, said English classes offer an important lifeline.

"It helps them to get … out of their loneliness, helps them to get out of despair," he said.

And it can help them achieve their goals.

Xu said it makes a big difference in accomplishing simple, everyday tasks.

"I want to go to the doctor, go … shopping, even help the people," she said.

Sabet smiles when he hears this. Learning English has given him a way to be generous, and now his student wants to do the same.

World.title: Feds approve Crawford Nickel Project in Ontario, promising it'll create 5,000 jobs during build
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has approved the Crawford Nickel Project in northern Ontario, saying the mine will draw in $5 billion in investment and create 5,000 jobs during its construction and another 1,300 when it is fully operating.

Located about 42 kilometres north of Timmins, Ont., the open-pit nickel-cobalt mine will have an extraction capacity of nearly 90 million tonnes of ore per year, contributing $70 billion to Canada's GDP over its expected 41-year lifespan.

The mine, which was referred to the federal government's Major Projects Office in November, is the first mine to be approved under Prime Minister Mark Carney's new impact assessment process.

The project was approved by Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin despite an impact assessment finding the project would negatively impact fish and bird habitats, water quality, Indigenous people and Canada's ability to meet its climate goals.

A news release explained Dabrusin's decision to approve the project came after determining that "the potential effects within federal jurisdiction are justified when taking into account the benefits this project will provide."

That doesn't mean concerns are being ignored; the Liberal government attached a number of legally binding conditions to the project that must be followed for as long as the mine is in operation.

Those conditions include taking steps to reduce adverse effects of the project on Indigenous communities that live in the area where the mine will be built.

A government statement said those measures include reducing any negative impacts on health, socio-economic conditions, physical and cultural heritage and the current use of land and resources for traditional purposes.

Managing tailings and further permits

Canada Nickel, the project's proponent, will have to construct a tailings management facility and ensure it is managed and tested throughout the life cycle of the mine.

"Canada's impact assessment process is designed to support well-planned projects that benefit communities," Dabrusin said in a statement.

"Through meaningful Indigenous engagement and evidence-based decision-making, it helps create the conditions for job creation, economic opportunity and responsible development."

Mark Selby, CEO of Canada Nickel said the mine's approval is an example of the responsible development of critical minerals because it involves a partnership with all levels of government and Indigenous people and maintains environmental standards.

Now that the project has been approved, Canada Nickel will continue crafting its engineering plan, gathering project financing and applying for further provincial and federal permits required before construction can begin.

World.title: Police left this survivor feeling blamed, broken. Now they're engaging with her again, and she's worried
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A woman who took part in mediation with the Ottawa Police Service in 2023 after struggling to report an historical sexual assault says the process left her feeling broken down and blamed, then placated and cast aside.

Keara Dean also says the reponse from police leaders after she called out the force at a public meeting in June has reinforced her belief that they're more interested in defending themselves and the institution than acknowledging mistakes, learning from them and repairing harm.

"The revictimization was beyond what I could have ever thought to have prepared for, and I work as a social worker and I've worked in this field," Dean said in an interview.

Recently Ottawa police asked Dean for the second time whether they can use her negative experience to help employees treat trauma survivors with more sensitivity. But Dean said she's worried that, like the first time police asked, it will not go well.

Cold cases break open

Dean's initial frustrations with the force began in November 2022, when she tried to assist with an investigation into a man charged that fall with sexually assaulting two women, murdering one of them and attempting to murder the other.

The alleged offences occurred in 2000 in Quebec City and Jonquière, Que.

Investigators announced there could be more victims. Some details reminded Dean, who lives in Ottawa, of a violent sexual assault she says she endured in Quebec City in the mid-1990s.

Dean called the tip line and said she was passed between police services in Quebec and Ottawa before being directed to report in person to police in Gatineau, Que.

By then, Dean said, she was angry and afraid to proceed, and she told the media about the mishandling of her calls.

An aerial view of the entrance to Ottawa Police Service headquarters at 474 Elgin St. in April. (Michel Aspirot/CBC)

'I was breaking down'

Ottawa police offered Dean mediation in spring 2023, and she said she was escorted into a locked room with two civilian employees of the reporting line and an officer from the professional standards section.

She had not been told she could bring a supporter or lawyer, and Dean said facing the members alone was her first indication that the process would not be trauma-informed.

During the session, Dean said, she was told that Ottawa police had given her the wrong information in 2022 "'because you didn't actually say on the reporting line that you were calling about historical sexual violence.'"

I had not stopped crying. I was in no state or frame of mind to sign anything. I couldn't even think of driving my vehicle. - Keara Dean

Dean said she felt blamed and attacked, and hit by a "flood of emotion" and shock.

She was certain she had used the words "historical sexual violence," she said, and remembered rehearsing them before picking up the phone.

"I was breaking down and crying," Dean said, and she couldn't stop crying after she left the room to use the washroom and returned.

Dean in a photograph taken in November 2022, shortly after she tried to report an historical sexual assault and was directed to contact multiple police forces. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

Flabbergasted

Dean said the two civilian employees left the room, leaving her with the professional standards officer.

The officer slid a piece of paper across the table and asked her to sign it, Dean said.

It was a form withdrawing the complaint Dean had made about Ottawa police to the Office of the Independent Police Review Director, now the Law Enforcement Complaints Agency.

The form had been filled out on her behalf in the first person, as though she had written the responses herself.

Dean was asked to sign this form, titled 'Withdrawal of a Public Complaint Against the Police,' which had been filled out for her. She had not said that she wanted to withdraw her complaint. (Ottawa Police Service/Keara Dean)

"I was, at this point, flabbergasted. I had not stopped crying. I was in no state or frame of mind to sign anything. I couldn't even think of driving my vehicle," Dean said.

She told the officer that asking her to sign the form was unethical, unprofessional and appalling, she recalled.

Dean refused to sign it, kept the document and provided a copy to CBC.

In an emailed statement, Ottawa police declined to answer questions about its mediation process in 2023, how mediation works today, whether it lived up to its own expectations and standards in preparing Dean for mediation, how the force prepares people now, whether the force regularly fills out withdrawal of complaint forms on behalf of people, and whether that's allowed or not.

The force said it "recognizes that Ms. Dean's experience, both when she initially contacted police in 2022 and during the subsequent public complaint process, caused her further distress."

Did say 'historical sexual violence'

A few months after the mediation, in summer 2023, Dean said another professional standards officer called her after listening to her initial call to the Ottawa police reporting line.

Dean said the officer confirmed she had used the words "historical sexual violence."

In September 2023, Dean received a formal letter of apology from Ottawa police, saying "the call taker and supervisor did not make sufficient inquiries of you or seek clarification on the information you provided to arrive at the correct response."

The apology letter ended the complaint process.

Dean said she later learned she could have filed a human rights complaint, but by then she had missed the deadline by one month.

Ottawa police declined to explain why Dean was told during mediation that she had not mentioned historical sexual violence.

The force said "a person reporting sexual violence should not be required to use specific terminology before their disclosure is recognized, properly assessed and responded to with care."

Addressed police board in June

Years later, Dean was among several residents who spoke about police misconduct at an Ottawa Police Service Board meeting this past June. She said she felt compelled to tell the board publicly that police didn't treat her with care, and that she believes the force continues to have difficulty responding appropriately to people reporting trauma.

After Dean finished her delegation, police Chief Eric Stubbs asked whether she would be willing to talk to employees about her experience to help educate them.

Dean said the force had made a similar request after mediation in 2023 but did not follow up, despite her contacting them twice.

I think training is crucial in this — hearing from victims themselves ... And we do that every time we have the opportunity to. - Deputy Chief Patricia Ferguson, later in meeting

"I felt like that was a ploy in mediation to make me feel better. So if you're actually, genuinely asking me to do something, I hope this time you're actually asking me and not … being performative, because last time it was crushing," Dean told Stubbs.

Deputy Chief Patricia Ferguson of the Ottawa Police Service in 2022. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

'Delegate was speaking about November 2022'

Ottawa police said in its emailed statement Thursday that Dean "should have received clearer communication" after the force offered her an opportunity to help train its members.

The force said it was reviewing why the followup did not happen and "what opportunities may remain to learn from her experience."

Later during the June police board meeting, board vice-chair and city Coun. Marty Carr asked what the force was doing to improve how it works with people who have experienced trauma.

"I did note that the delegate was speaking about November 2022. I would say that since then we have made some strides," Deputy Chief Patricia Ferguson replied.

"I think training is crucial in this — hearing from victims themselves, first-hand stories about how the impact of the treatment that they received from our members is very significant. And we do that every time we have the opportunity to, so that we can give that feedback to our officers."

Dean said Ferguson was wrong to characterize the force's handling of her case as an issue limited to November 2022.

She said the lack of a trauma-informed approach continued during the mediation in spring 2023 and after the apology that fall, when police did not respond to her followups about helping with training and later told her all available spots had been filled.

Dean said Ferguson's comments left her feeling "dismissed."

She also said they reinforced her concerns about whether the police force was capable of meaningful change and whether it intended to follow through on its latest request for her help.

The changes made since 2022 do not erase what occurred or lessen the need for [Ottawa police] to continue listening, learning, and improving how it supports victims of sexual violence. - Ottawa police statement

Ottawa police said Ferguson's response to Carr's question was "not intended to minimize Ms. Dean's experience."

"We recognize, however, that the comments did not land that way for Ms. Dean and may have left her feeling that her experience was being dismissed. The changes made since 2022 do not erase what occurred or lessen the need for [Ottawa police] to continue listening, learning, and improving how it supports victims of sexual violence."

World.title: Debate over trans athletes overtakes WNBA
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The WNBA has been on a meteoric rise the last few years. It's so popular it just signed media rights deals worth $3.1 billion US.

But with that explosion in popularity and cultural cachet has come the projection of larger culture war issues onto the league.

The latest? The debate over trans athletes in sports.

It started earlier this month, when Indiana Fever sharpshooter Sophie Cunningham ignited an online firestorm after an ESPN profile quoted her voicing support for barring transgender girls and women from women's sports.

"I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think, with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men," Cunningham said.

The issue — which has been a major point of contention in the U.S. for more than a year now after President Donald Trump signed an executive order preventing trans people from participating in women's or girls' sporting events — remained a focal point during Tuesday's matchup between the Fever and Seattle Storm.

Rally outside game renews controversy

Outside the arena, there was a small rally in support of Cunningham's comments and pushing for a proposal currently on the ballot in the state of Washington that would bar transgender students from competing in girls' athletics at school ( the Supreme Court upheld similar laws in Idaho and West Virginia last month ).

Inside the arena, a Storm player wore a trans rights shirt ahead of playing. Cunningham was booed throughout the game, according to ESPN . And the co-owner of the Storm, Celeste Keaton, got suspended for five home games for allegedly cursing out two fans wearing t-shirts with XX and XY chromosomes in support of Cunningham.

The Storm apologized for Keaton's comments and said in a statement: "Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome, and we remain committed to creating an inclusive environment where every fan is treated with respect."

People rally to support Cunningham and her comments outside Tuesday's game. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Cunningham weighed in as well, posting on social media: "Truly embarrassing of the co-owner. Unfortunately shows the type of leader she is."

She also wrote, "I truly believe there is a safe space and love for EVERYBODY. Biological girls, biological boys, trans women, and trans men. Everyone is welcome at my table! You can disagree and still be kind."

The events at the Tuesday game and Cunningham's initial comments have been fodder on Fox News. White House spokesperson Karoline Leavitt also weighed in, saying it was "astonishing" to see the backlash Cunningham was receiving from "Democrats and left-wing figures across the country."

"Men should not be playing in women's sports. It's completely ludicrous that anyone could support that."

More people gathered in support of Cunningham outside the game Tuesday. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Politics 'a lightning rod'

Trans rights has been a longtime pet issue for the Trump White House. In the lead up to the 2024 election Trump ran an ad attacking Kamala Harris's support for gender-affirming care for trans people. The campaign focused on NFL and college football.

"I think anything political from an athlete right now, particularly around race, around transgender issues, it's going to become a lightning rod right now," said Molly Yanity, the director of the sports media and communication program at the University of Rhode Island. She said Cunningham is particularly high profile and on social media, including Reddit, has earned the nickname "MAGA Barbie" — fair or not.

"[Cunningham] hasn't really come out with any, let's say, progressive, kind of politics. So I think that the absence of her saying anything opens the door to assumptions that she is on the other side of that."

While the Indiana Fever came out saying neither the organization nor Cunningham had any knowledge of the demonstration at the arena Tuesday, Alejandra Caraballo, a clinical instructor at the Harvard Law Cyberlaw Clinic who frequently speaks about trans rights, sees the WNBA's suspension of the Storm's co-owner as a kind of green light for protesters to keep bringing politics to the sport.

"They're saying they're there to support Sophie, but what they're really there to do is support a transphobic message," she said. "They're intentionally trying to go to these events to get reactions to film and create content and further this controversy and bring attention."

Not WNBA's first brush with controversy

This isn't the first time the WNBA has found itself at the nexus of American culture wars.

Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas said she had received death threats and been called racial slurs for making contact with star player Caitlin Clark's throat during a game in June . Republican lawmakers have recently fuelled the controversy by writing a letter in early July saying they were concerned by reports that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated."

Attendees at Tuesday's game hold a sign referencing Cunningham's comments. (Steve Bisig/Imagin Images/Reuters)

Yanity thinks a lot of the controversy is being drummed up by fans, not the players. And then are being discussed ad nauseum on social media.

"It has become a very, very toxic place where threats of violence have been made against specifically the Black players."

The league has faced criticism that they are not doing enough to protect players from the online onslaught. Last week, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert called the online abuse "unacceptable," saying "The racism, the misogyny, the homophobia, the harassment, and threats directed to our players, has no place in sport or anywhere else."

The WNBA did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CBC.

WATCH | Supreme Court upholds U.S. laws banning trans athletes: SCOTUS upholds laws banning trans athletes from women's school sports | Duration 1:16 The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favour of overturning the decisions of lower courts that found laws in Idaho and West Virginia banning transgender athletes from competing in women's sports at the school level violated the U.S. Constitution and a federal anti-discrimination law. The 6-3 ruling to uphold the laws in Idaho and West Virginia opens the pathway for as many as 29 other states to pursue laws that limit the participation of trans athletes in women’s sports.

Ultimately, said Yanity, this is a league that has seen explosive growth over the last several years. "It used to be that you'd have to search high and low to find the games. [Now] they are all readily available and at your fingertips. … These social aspects of the game are also being analyzed."

To add to that, she said politics are inherent to women's sport, pointing to the fact that it took an act of Congress in the U.S. and a president's signature for women to even get on the court and have a somewhat even playing field.

"Everything about a woman's existence, and particularly a Black woman's existence, is political."

World.title: Hamas will hand over weapons under Gaza peace deal only if Israel withdraws forces, ends attacks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Implementing the peace deal for Gaza announced by U.S. President Donald Trump will depend on Israel first meeting its commitments under an agreement reached last year, including withdrawing its army from the territory, Hamas said in a statement Friday.

Trump announced a "major milestone" toward ending the war in Gaza on Thursday, saying his Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups.

The announcement followed months of faltering efforts to keep the ceasefire agreement reached in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, last year on track, and it wasn't immediately clear how strongly either Hamas or Israel stood behind it.

Previous attempts to reach an agreement have foundered amid mutual suspicion and each side's insistence that the other must move first.

Hamas said Friday the first step must be a commitment by Israel "to stopping the killing" and fully withdrawing from the Gaza Strip.

Meanwhile, an Israeli official, speaking to Reuters on condition they not be identified, said Israel's position remained that "there will be no withdrawal whatsoever," past the current, agreed-upon Yellow Line, "unless Hamas undergoes a genuine disarmament."

WATCH | Disarmament, with conditions: Hamas agrees to disarm under Trump's new Gaza peace deal, if Israel withdraws forces | Duration 5:41 U.S. President Donald Trump says an agreement has been reached for the complete disarmament of Hamas in Gaza. A senior Hamas official agreed to the plan Friday, but said it depends on Israel withdrawing its forces and ending attacks.

Within hours, Gaza medical authorities said several Palestinians had been wounded in an Israeli airstrike in the enclave. There was no immediate comment from the Israeli military.

On the ground, Gazans, still struggling with basic survival after the Israeli military campaign in response to the deadly 2023 Hamas attack on Israel devastated the enclave, remained skeptical, saying little had changed.

Inside a tent encampment in Gaza City, where women were busy filling plastic jerrycans with water, displaced Palestinians urged Trump to compel Israel to abide by the agreement.

"You, Trump, you should start it from your end, ceasefire, stop the assassinations and complete the Israeli army's withdrawal from the Gaza Strip," said 60-year-old Samir Ayad.

"We are not seeing any agreement at all, nothing from what he [Trump] is saying," he said.

'Difficult and painful'

Ghazi Hamad, a Hamas official involved in the negotiations, said earlier the group was ready to accept an agreement he called "difficult and painful."

But he avoided using the term "disarmament" and said the agreement was a "comprehensive framework" that would depend on Israel implementing the first phase of the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement.

That would mean withdrawing its forces to where they stood in October and letting in more goods and aid.

Only then would Hamas agree to hand over its weapons to the new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body set up to run the enclave.

"We insisted to the mediators that Israel must abide by the agreement," he said.

WATCH | Former Canadian ambassador to Israel 'highly skeptical' of deal: 'I’m highly skeptical,' says former ambassador to Israel on Trump's Gaza peace deal | Duration 8:02 Hamas has agreed to a disarmament plan, according to the Gaza Board of Peace, but only if Israel withdraws from the territory. Former Canadian ambassador to Israel Jon Allen is 'highly skeptical' about the deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, saying the president has made many promises, but significant controversy remains over the outcome.

On Friday, the NCAG published what it said was the 15-point plan, which called on both Israel and Hamas, together with other Palestinian factions, to implement fully the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement, in particular the end to military operations in Gaza.

The document outlined steps to allow the NCAG to assume responsibility for civil governance in Gaza, and said it would oversee a process to "decommission and store heavy weapons, military production sites, depots of weapons, and tunnels."

The process "shall be linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases, from the areas under its control in Gaza," it said, adding that no weapons would be handed over to Israel or non-Palestinian parties.

The NCAG said it was ready to assume its responsibilities, while Germany, a major donor, said it would do its part to help the agreement.

On Tuesday, Trump met in Washington with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an election in October in which he may need the support of right-wing parties that have rejected previous deals in Gaza.

The Israeli source said the issue of Gaza did not come up during Netanyahu's meeting with Trump.

World.title: Cooling hot subways in NYC with Canadian tech
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it's Emily. I'm always amazed by how hot it can get in subway stations. So the idea of cooling them by taking that heat to use elsewhere seems, well, cool to me. I've written about heating buildings with waste heat from places like nuclear power plants , paper mills and sewers . So why not subways?

This week:

Canadian tech aims to cool hot subways in New York City

The Big Picture: How wildfires generate thunderclouds

What is 'wishcycling' and why are some municipalities cracking down on it?

Canadian tech aims to cool hot subways in New York City

A woman holds a hand-held fan on a subway platform during a heat wave in New York City in June 2025. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters)

Underground subway stations are hot and getting hotter, drawing complaints from transit riders around the world . That includes those in Canadian cities such as Montreal , where a reporter recently measured the temperature as 38 C.

Now a Canadian company is testing an energy-efficient cooling solution in New York City's subway system.

Toronto-based Cascara Energy and New York City's Metropolitan Transportation Authority are installing the radiant cooling system in ceiling arches in East Broadway station. The first units are expected to be running at the end of August and the pilot will continue until the end of 2027.

The system uses loops of chilled water-filled pipes to absorb heat and make passengers feel cooler as they pass underneath.

"The effect is similar to the experience of walking through the refrigerator aisle at a supermarket," said Lucas Bejarno, a spokesperson for the MTA in an email.

The cooling system will consist of loops of pipes full of chilled water that will be installed in ceiling arches in East Broadway station. (Megan Armas/MTA)

Unlike traditional air conditioning, it doesn't use any fans, making it more compact. It also promises to be easier to maintain and 25 to 35 per cent more efficient.

The hope is that the system won't just keep passengers more comfortable but that the heat could be recovered and recycled for other uses, the MTA reported in its October 2025 Climate Resilience Roadmap .

Why subway systems are so hot

There are many sources of heat in a subway system, including people, electronics such as lighting and screens and train braking and air conditioning systems.

Robert Croghan, founder and CEO of Cascara Energy, said normally the walls of the subway can absorb a lot of that heat, but at some point they can't take in any more. His system aims to catch new heat before it hits the walls as well as gradually cool the walls themselves over time to restore their ability to absorb more heat.

Meanwhile, the heat recovered by the system can be carried away and used elsewhere.

"You're mining the heat," he said.

A goal of the project is to see how much heat can be "mined" and available to heat water and buildings.

Croghan said that wouldn't just displace burning fossil fuels for heat. It's also far more efficient than drilling boreholes for geothermal heatin g, which also uses underground heat.

"There is waste heat everywhere," he said. "We don't need to be drilling for it."

A diagram shows how passengers would be cooled and heat would be removed in the East Broadway station pilot project in New York City. (Cascara Energy)

Heat is already recycled from the London Underground

The London Underground is already collecting waste heat from the Northern line tunnels of its network year-round in the British capital for its Bunhill 2 Energy Centre , located in the former City Road station. That, in turn, is one of the heat sources for a district heating network connected to thousands of homes, a school and two community centres. The system's fan can be reversed in the summer to pump cool air into the tunnels.

WATCH | Can this building save the London Underground from overheating?:

Croghan said that's a more conventional cooling system with high-velocity fans, so it uses more energy than his company's passive radiant cooling technology. The MTA notes that such conventional systems also need more space for mechanical rooms and street-level cooling towers.

London and New York are especially notorious for their steamy subways, but could recovering heat from subway tunnels and stations also work in Canada?

"For sure. Absolutely," Croghan said.

He hopes the New York pilot, which his company is mostly funding itself, will show the system works and get other transit systems interested.

– Emily Chung

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode: With people on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border choking on smoke, much of it coming from fires in Canada's forests, U.S. President Donald Trump is threatening new, fire-related tariffs in retaliation. Climate scientists like Zeke Hausfather say wildfires in Canada’s boreal forest are linked to global warming, but as environmental law expert Godwin Dzah explains, when health hazards cross borders, there are ways to hold governments and companies to account. But the question of liability gets hazy when climate change enters the conversation.

Reader feedback

Dan Kells, who lives North Saanich, B.C., wrote in to say, “The story by Nicole Mortillaro about purchasing a used EV is important to help assuage many fears that have been falsely created about EVs. First-person accounts are probably the best way to alleviate some of those fears.

“I am attaching a photo of our 2014 Leaf with a trailer attached. The carmaker recommends a small utility trailer only if you must tow, so we may have pushed the limit a bit here on our moving day.

“I was inspired to write to you because of Nicole's story and I would like to assure her and all Canadians that an EV is a solid, reliable vehicle that has excellent range in the newer models at the same time as we have an ever-expanding charging infrastructure. In fact, B.C. Hydro just announced a tripling of their EV charging infrastructure.”

(Dan Kells)

Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there too!)

The Big Picture: How wildfires generate thunderclouds

A huge fire in southwest France has generated the country's first recorded pyrocumulonimbus fire cloud. While they're rare in Europe, Canada has a reputation for producing the most fire thunderclouds in the world, most recently during the Boston Bar fire in B.C.

The diagram shows how wildfires generate these unusual clouds: The heat from a wildfire causes hot air to rise in an updraft, pulling moisture, smoke and even burning embers up with it. Because the atmosphere is cooler higher up, at some point the vapour and smoke cool and spread out, and the water condenses into a cloud above the smoke column.

When they grow large enough, pyrocumulonimbus clouds start to behave like thunderstorm clouds in other ways, generating strong, erratic winds and lightning. Read more about pyrocumulonimbus clouds and how they can pose a danger during wildfires .

— Emily Chung

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

Replacing the gas-burning version of this appliance with electric can help people with asthma as much as some drugs , drastically reducing hospital admissions, a new study finds.

Using AI chatbots? Knowable suggests four user tips that can cut down on the amount of energy your AI queries suck up .

Critics worry EVs will crash the grid, but an emerging EV technology will actually help support the grid and make electricity more reliable and more affordable.

When you’re stuck in the Strait of Hormuz, you can pick up many hitchhikers — and scientists warn that’s a biodiversity “super-spreader” threat.

What is 'wishcycling' and why are some municipalities cracking down on it?

‘Contaminating’ recyclables with non-recyclable garbage makes it harder to sell paper, plastic and glass to end markets where they can be recycled into new material. (Maggie MacPherson/CBC)

Have you been "wishcycling?"

The word is a portmanteau of "wishful thinking" and "recycling" and is an ongoing challenge for recycling systems.

“Wishcycling is when we see residents or people using the recycling carts throwing material in them that is not recycling in the hopes that somehow the material will end up where it needs to be," Ben Routledge, the Regional District of Nanaimo's manager of solid waste services, told CBC's On the Island.

It's become such an issue in the Nanaimo, B.C., area that officials are looking at fines for scofflaws.

Recycle B.C., the non-profit that manages residential packaging and paper recycling across the province, says slightly less than six per cent of the loads it receives are contaminated.

Routledge says the most common "wishcycled" items are things that can be recycled through a depot but don't belong in curbside collection bins, like woven plastic or zipper lock bags. Improperly cleaned containers are also common.

But he says the region is also seeing an alarming increase in scrap metal, household appliances and even hazardous waste like propane tanks, batteries or bear spray.

How to fix a dangerous, costly problem?

“All of that stuff can [mistakenly be put] into a collection truck, which is being compacted," he said. "And those hazardous [wastes] can either contaminate the material around them, they can explode or they can ignite.”

Contamination makes it harder to sell paper, plastic and glass to end markets where they're recycled into new material. Loads that are seriously contaminated may end up in the landfill.

Recycle B.C. sets its acceptable contamination threshold at five per cent.

The Regional District of Nanaimo has seen the rate of contamination in its recycling loads climb from four per cent to 5.4 per cent over the last year and a half, with some loads topping 18 per cent, Routledge said.

As a result, outreach teams will start issuing warnings for non-compliance. After three strikes, residents will face a $500 fine — and if they persist, the district will consider stopping pickups.

The City of Richmond, south of Vancouver, is also auditing residents’ bins after its contamination rate climbed to 7.3 per cent for curbside pickup and 11.3 per cent for multifamily residences. People who break the rules will find an "oops" sticker slapped on their blue box.

Getting those numbers down matters — if municipalities let contamination rates rise too high, they can face hefty financial penalties.

"If it stays above the allowable threshold for too long of a period of time, we can face financial penalties that could equal as much as $120,000 per year," Routledge said.

Recycle B.C. says when a municipality's contamination routinely exceeds its thresholds, its first step is to work with the community.

"Financial penalties are only considered if contamination remains persistently high after those extended efforts," the non-profit told CBC News in an email.

If you're unsure about whether something you're throwing out belongs in your recycling bin, check with your local recycling service. In B.C., you can check RecycleBC.ca or download the Recycle B.C. app.

— Simon Little

World.title: De la Espriella desists from holding swearing-in ceremony at military base
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella has apparently given up trying to be sworn in before the military and asked Congress to allow the ceremony to take place in Cali, Colombia’s third largest city.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said Sunday that volcanic activity made travel to Popayan, the capital of Cauca, made a “secure, well-organized” inauguration ceremony all but impossible.

“For this reason, I respectfully ask the honorable House of Representatives, which has not yet debated my inauguration in a plenary session, to convene the August 7th session in the city of Cali,” said the president-elect.

“As soon as I am sworn in as president of the republic, my government’s first security council will be held in the Marco Fidel Suarez airbase in the city of Cali,” added De la Espriella, suggesting he has given up his aspiration to be sworn in inside a military base.

In an interview, Santiago de Cali University president Carlos Andres Perez, told Blu Radio on Tuesday that Valle del Cauca Governor Dilian Francisca Toro told him the university theater would be used for the inauguration.

Following the main ceremony, De la Espriella will travel to the Pichincha Military Canton, the base of the 3rd Division, to assume his role as supreme commander of the armed forces.

The apparent decision to desist from a military inauguration comes after major tensions with the outgoing government of President Gustavo Petro, who ordered the military not to cooperate with his elected successor.

An inauguration at a military base was also opposed by the Democratic Center, the largest political party in De la Espriella’s far-right congressional coalition.

The opponents claimed that Colombia’s constitution submits the armed forces to civilian authority. A swearing-in ceremony before them would have been confusing and inappropriate.

According to De la Espriella, his intention meant to stress his support for the Colombia’s “heroes.”

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.content:
Heavy rain, strong winds, and snowfall expected as new frontal system approaches

SANTIAGO â Chile’s central and southern regions are preparing for a powerful frontal system bringing wind, rain, and snow over the coming days, according to updated forecasts from the DirecciÃ³n MeteorolÃ³gica de Chile (DMC). The system is expected to benefit water reserves, with substantial snowfall anticipated across the Andes from the Coquimbo to BiobÃ­o regions.

The DMC has issued weather alerts for much of central Chile due to moderate to strong winds and heavy precipitation. Gusts may exceed 80 km/h in areas from ValparaÃ­so to Ãuble, driven by a low-level jet stream. Meteorologists are closely monitoring the development of a second system forecast to impact central Chile on Sunday, June 15. Early estimates suggest additional rainfall of up to 40 mm for ValparaÃ­so and the Santiago Metropolitan Region, which may exacerbate soil saturation and pose travel disruptions if storms continue in quick succession.

World.title: Universidad de Chile Eliminated by Curicó Unido in Copa Chile Upset
World.content:
CuricÃ³ Unido advances to quarterfinals after dramatic second-leg draw

SANTIAGO â Defending champions Universidad de Chile have been eliminated from the Copa Chile Coca Cola Sin AzÃºcar 2025 after a 2-2 draw against CuricÃ³ Unido on Wednesday night at Estadio Nacional. The aggregate score favored the visitors, who secured a surprising quarterfinal berth.

Early hopes fade for Universidad de Chile

The home side, managed by Gustavo Ãlvarez, entered the match trailing 2-1 from the first leg. With the return of key players from international duty, including NicolÃ¡s FernÃ¡ndez, MatÃ­as SepÃºlveda, and Maximiliano Guerrero, the team hoped to reverse the deficit.

Universidad de Chile dominated early proceedings, creating multiple chances in the first 15 minutes. However, CuricÃ³ Unido, led by head coach HÃ©ctor Almandoz, resisted pressure and posed threats on the counterattack.

After a series of missed opportunities, MatÃ­as Zaldivia broke the deadlock for the hosts in the 37th minute, leveling the aggregate score and reigniting the home crowdâs hopes.

The second half started disastrously for Universidad de Chile. Within seconds, Ian Aliaga unleashed a powerful shot from distance to restore CuricÃ³ Unido’s aggregate lead. Though Universidad de Chile continued to press, they struggled to break through CuricÃ³ Unidoâs defense. Substitute Lucas Assadi managed to equalize in stoppage time (90+1′), but the late goal was not enough to save their title defense.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Full Moon in June 2025: Date, Meaning, and What’s Ahead in the Night Sky
World.content:
The full moon in June 2025 will occur on Wednesday, June 11, and will be visible in most regions depending on local moonrise and moonset times. Known as the Strawberry Moon, this lunar event is tied to Native American traditions marking the ripening of wild strawberries and the approach of summer in the Northern Hemisphere.

In Argentina, for example, the moon will rise around 5:52 p.m. and set at 9:19 a.m. on June 12. This full moon, like others throughout the year, has long held cultural, astrological, and even emotional significance. While there is no scientific consensus on its effects, itâs commonly associated with heightened emotions, sleep disturbances, and symbolic transitions.
