Operating Strength in Mexico’s Industrial Heartland

Fibra Uno, known locally as FUNO and structured as a FIBRA – Mexico’s equivalent of a US REIT – reported portfolio occupancy of 95.8% at the close of the June quarter.

The average occupancy rate across the period was even higher, reaching 96.1%, underscoring resilient demand for its vast industrial and commercial footprint.

Year-on-year occupancy gains were particularly notable in key northern and western industrial hubs, including Monterrey, Guadalajara, and Reynosa.

These cities are critical nodes in nearshoring supply chains, attracting foreign manufacturers relocating operations closer to the US consumer market.

For expat investors unfamiliar with the geography, Monterrey serves as Mexico’s industrial capital, while Guadalajara is the country’s tech and innovation center.

Reynosa, located directly on the Texas border, is a high-traffic logistics and maquiladora zone that benefits directly from US-Mexico trade flows.

Reading the Fibra Uno Results

Same-store cash net operating income, a key gauge of organic growth that strips out acquisitions, jumped 13.1% compared to the same quarter in 2025.

This double-digit expansion signals that FUNO is extracting more value from its existing portfolio through rent escalations and operational efficiencies.

Tenant retention registered at 60.8% during the quarter, a figure that reflects a deliberate portfolio rotation strategy rather than weakness.

Management has been selectively replacing lower-credit tenants with higher-quality occupants, a process that temporarily pressures retention rates but improves long-term cash flow stability.

The trust’s diversified tenant base spans industrial parks, retail plazas, and office towers, though industrial assets now dominate the income mix.

Foreign investors should note that FUNO’s certificates, called CBFIs, trade on the Mexican Bolsa under the ticker FUNO11 and offer direct exposure to hard commercial property assets.

A logistics warehouse. Fibra Uno is Mexico’s largest property trust. (Photo: internal archive)

FFO Growth and the Net Income Swing

Funds from operations per CBFI, the industry-standard metric that adds back non-cash charges to net income, reached US$0.0613 in the second quarter.

This represents a 4.8% increase from the US$0.0585 recorded a year earlier, confirming that cash-generating capacity improved.

However, the headline net income per certificate swung to a negative US$0.0285, a sharp contrast to the positive US$0.0915 posted in Q2 2025.

The reversal stemmed entirely from non-operating factors, primarily valuation adjustments on the property portfolio and financial instruments, not from any deterioration in rental operations.

Real-estate trusts routinely mark their assets to market, and in periods of rising interest rates or cap-rate expansion, book values can decline even as rent checks keep arriving.

This accounting dynamic is critical for international investors to understand: the operating business performed well, but paper losses on asset values dragged the bottom-line figure into the red.

What the Numbers Mean for International Investors

For expatriates and foreign capital allocators, the Fibra Uno results present a clear investment narrative: strong property fundamentals coexist with quarterly net-income volatility.

Occupancy above 95% in a portfolio of this scale – FUNO is Mexico’s largest REIT by asset value – provides a margin of safety that smaller trusts cannot match.

The 13.1% same-store growth indicates that in-place leases are repricing upward, a direct hedge against Mexico’s inflationary environment.

Investors should monitor the trust’s distribution policy, as FIBRAs are required to distribute a high percentage of taxable income to certificate holders, creating a yield-oriented total return profile.

The negative net result per certificate does not automatically threaten distributions, because FFO and cash available for distribution are the relevant payout metrics.

Nevertheless, sustained valuation declines could eventually pressure book equity and refinancing conditions, making the next few quarters’ appraisal cycles worth watching closely.

Market Context and Nearshoring Tailwinds

FUNO’s operational resilience arrives against a backdrop of sustained nearshoring investment flowing into Mexico’s industrial real-estate market.

Global manufacturers continue to expand production capacity in border states and the Bajío region, absorbing warehouse and logistics space at rates that outpace new construction.

The trust’s geographic footprint aligns closely with these demand corridors, positioning it as a direct beneficiary of supply-chain reconfiguration away from Asia.

Currency dynamics also matter: foreign investors holding CBFIs earn rental income denominated in Mexican pesos, which have historically offered carry-trade appeal against the US dollar.

At the current exchange rate of approximately 18.5 pesos per US dollar, the trust’s US-dollar-denominated FFO provides a transparent earnings stream for international analysis.

While global interest-rate uncertainty persists, FUNO’s scale and diversified tenant roster offer a degree of insulation that smaller, single-market REITs in Latin America often lack.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Fibra Uno and how does it relate to a US REIT?

Fibra Uno, or FUNO, is Mexico’s largest FIBRA, a real-estate investment trust structured similarly to a US REIT. It owns and operates industrial, retail, and office properties, and its certificates (CBFIs) trade on the Mexican stock exchange, offering investors liquid exposure to commercial real estate.

Why did Fibra Uno report a net loss per certificate despite high occupancy?

The negative net income per CBFI of US$0.0285 resulted from non-operating valuation adjustments on the property portfolio and financial instruments, not from weak rental operations. Funds from operations, which reflect cash earnings, actually rose 4.8% year-on-year to US$0.0613 per certificate.

How does nearshoring affect Fibra Uno’s business?

Nearshoring drives demand for industrial and logistics space in northern Mexico, particularly in cities like Monterrey and Reynosa where FUNO owns significant assets. This trend supports occupancy rates and rent growth, directly benefiting the trust’s same-store income performance.

World.title: Megacable Earnings Rise 11% as Mexican Cable Firm Nears 6M Users
World.content:
Companies · Mexico

Key Facts —Net Profit MXN$852 million (~US$46 million), up 11% year-on-year —Internet Subscribers Close to 6 million, with roughly 5.9 million reported and 101,000 net additions —Revenue Record quarterly revenues driven by broadband growth —Strategic Focus Accelerating full migration to fiber optic infrastructure —Market Position Major Mexican cable-TV, internet, and telecom operator

Megacable earnings climbed 11% in the second quarter of 2026, as the Mexican telecom operator pushed its internet subscriber base close to 6 million. Net profit reached MXN$852 million (~US$46 million), reflecting steady growth in broadband adoption and a strategic shift toward fiber optic technology.

Fibre-optic cabling. Megacable is accelerating its shift to fibre. (Photo: internal archive)

Financial Performance and Subscriber Growth

The Guadalajara-based company reported record quarterly revenues during the period, though it did not disclose the exact top-line figure in its preliminary release. The profit expansion was anchored by a 9.1% year-on-year increase in internet subscribers, which now total roughly 5.9 million.

Net additions in the recent quarter reached approximately 101,000, underscoring consistent demand for fixed-line broadband in Mexico. The company’s ability to grow its base in a competitive market has drawn attention from international investors tracking Latin American telecom assets.

Megacable, formally known as Megacable Holdings S.A.B. de C.V., is one of Mexico’s largest cable and internet providers. It competes directly with Carlos Slim’s América Móvil and the satellite service Sky, offering bundled television, broadband, and telephony services.

The 11% profit increase translates to a net income of MXN$852 million (~US$46 million), up from approximately MXN$768 million in the same period last year. This growth rate signals operational leverage as the company scales its high-margin fiber network.

Inside the Megacable Earnings Report

Central to the Megacable earnings story is an accelerated migration to fiber optic infrastructure. The company is replacing legacy coaxial cable with fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) technology, a capital-intensive process that promises higher speeds, lower maintenance costs, and improved customer retention.

Fiber optics deliver symmetrical upload and download speeds, a critical advantage as remote work and streaming consumption remain elevated across Latin America. For foreign investors, this infrastructure upgrade represents a long-term moat against competitors who rely on older copper or hybrid networks.

The full shift to fiber is not yet complete, but the pace has quickened noticeably in 2026. Megacable is prioritizing high-density urban zones where the return on investment is fastest, before extending the build-out to secondary cities.

Industry analysts note that pure fiber networks typically reduce churn and allow operators to upsell higher-tier plans. This dynamic supports average revenue per user (ARPU) growth, a metric closely watched by portfolio managers evaluating emerging-market telecom stocks.

Telecom infrastructure. Megacable’s internet base is nearing 6 million. (Photo: internal archive)

Competitive Landscape in Mexican Telecom

Mexico’s telecommunications market is dominated by América Móvil, which controls roughly 60% of mobile and fixed-line subscribers through its Telmex and Telcel brands. Megacable has carved out a regional stronghold, particularly in the Bajío region and parts of Mexico City’s metropolitan area.

The company’s focus on bundled services – combining internet, cable TV, and phone – has proven resilient even as streaming platforms erode traditional television viewership. Megacable has responded by offering integrated packages that include access to Netflix and other over-the-top services.

Foreign expatriates and retirees living in Mexico often encounter Megacable as a primary provider in cities like Guadalajara, León, and Querétaro. The company’s service quality and pricing are frequent topics in expat forums, where reliable internet is a top priority.

Regulatory oversight from Mexico’s Federal Telecommunications Institute (IFT) continues to shape the competitive dynamics. Recent rulings have aimed to reduce barriers for smaller operators, potentially benefiting Megacable as it expands its fiber footprint beyond its traditional territory.

Investment Implications and Capital Expenditure

The fiber build-out requires significant capital expenditure, which investors should monitor in upcoming quarterly filings. Megacable has historically funded expansion through a mix of operating cash flow and debt, maintaining a leverage profile that rating agencies consider manageable.

A stronger Mexican peso, which traded at approximately 18.5 per US dollar during the quarter, can influence the company’s equipment import costs. Much of the fiber optic hardware is sourced from international suppliers and priced in US dollars.

For US dollar-denominated investors, the peso’s relative stability in 2026 has reduced currency risk compared to more volatile Latin American markets like Argentina or Venezuela. Megacable’s revenue is entirely peso-denominated, making FX movements a secondary but relevant consideration.

The company’s shares trade on the Mexican Stock Exchange (BMV) under the ticker MEGA.CPO. International investors can gain exposure through exchange-traded funds focused on Mexican equities or Latin American telecommunications.

Broader Trends in Latin American Connectivity

Megacable’s performance mirrors a regional trend of rapid broadband adoption. Across Latin America, fixed-line internet penetration has surged since the pandemic, with fiber optic connections growing faster than any other technology.

Governments from Brazil to Colombia have launched public-private partnerships to expand digital infrastructure, but private operators like Megacable remain the primary drivers of last-mile connectivity. The company’s subscriber growth of 9.1% outpaces Mexico’s population growth, indicating deeper market penetration.

For expatriates and digital nomads considering relocation to Mexico, the availability of high-speed fiber internet is often a deciding factor. Cities with robust Megacable coverage are increasingly marketed as remote-work hubs, competing with better-known destinations like Medellín or Buenos Aires.

The company’s record revenues suggest that demand for premium broadband tiers is strengthening, even as inflationary pressures affect household budgets. This resilience underscores the essential nature of internet access in modern Latin American economies.

Outlook and Strategic Priorities

Looking ahead, Megacable’s management has signaled that the fiber migration will remain the top strategic priority through at least 2027. The company aims to convert its entire footprint, though a specific completion timeline has not been publicly disclosed.

Investors will closely watch the next quarterly report for updates on capital expenditure, ARPU trends, and any impact from Mexico’s broader economic conditions. The country’s GDP growth, projected at around 2% for 2026, provides a stable but unspectacular backdrop for consumer spending.

The milestone of 6 million internet subscribers appears imminent, with the current base sitting at roughly 5.9 million. Crossing that threshold would likely generate positive headlines and could serve as a catalyst for the stock.

For The Rio Times readership – comprising expats, investors, and business professionals with interests in Latin America – Megacable represents a pure-play bet on Mexico’s digital transformation. The company’s steady execution and fiber-focused strategy offer a contrast to more volatile sectors like mining or oil.

Frequently Asked Questions

What were Megacable’s Q2 2026 earnings results?

Megacable reported an 11% increase in net profit to MXN$852 million (~US$46 million) for the second quarter of 2026, driven by record revenues and strong internet subscriber growth.

How many internet subscribers does Megacable have?

Megacable’s internet subscriber base is close to 6 million, with roughly 5.9 million reported. The company added approximately 101,000 net subscribers in the recent quarter, representing 9.1% year-on-year growth.

What is Megacable’s fiber optic strategy?

Megacable is accelerating a full migration from legacy coaxial cable to fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) technology. This capital-intensive upgrade aims to deliver higher speeds, reduce maintenance costs, and improve customer retention across its Mexican footprint.

World.title: CFE Profit Drops 43% as a Weak Peso Hits Mexico’s Utility
World.content:
Markets · Mexico

Key Facts —Q2 Net Profit MXN$48,026 million (~US$2.75 billion), down 43.4% year-on-year. —Revenue Q2 revenues slipped 1.2% to MXN$172,570 million (~US$9.88 billion). —FX Impact A sharp drop in foreign-exchange gains, driven by peso depreciation, hit the bottom line. —Operational Strength First-half EBITDA hit MXN$119,022 million, the highest H1 level since 2018. —Debt Exposure 52% of CFE’s debt is denominated in foreign currency, mostly US dollars.

CFE profit fell 43.4 percent in the second quarter of 2026, as Mexico’s state-owned electric utility absorbed heavy foreign-exchange losses from a weaker peso. Net income dropped to MXN$48,026 million (~US$2.75 billion) from MXN$84,783 million (~US$4.85 billion) a year earlier, the company reported on July 30.

High-voltage transmission lines. Mexico’s CFE saw Q2 profit fall on a weaker peso. (Photo: internal archive)

The Currency Blow to the Bottom Line

The Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), Mexico’s state-owned power monopoly, generates its revenue in pesos but carries substantial dollar-denominated debt.

The company disclosed that 52 percent of its total debt is in foreign currency, primarily US dollars.

When the peso depreciates against the dollar, the peso value of that debt and associated interest payments rises, creating paper losses.

In the second quarter, a sharp reduction in foreign-exchange gains compared to the prior year was the primary driver of the profit decline.

This accounting effect overshadowed what was otherwise a period of solid operational performance for the utility.

What Drove the CFE Profit Decline

Total revenues for the April-to-June period dipped 1.2 percent to MXN$172,570 million (~US$9.88 billion).

For the first half of 2026, revenues reached MXN$332,229 million, a 2.2 percent decrease from the same period in 2025.

Despite the top-line softness, CFE demonstrated significant cost discipline.

The cost of sales fell 8.4 percent during the first half, helping gross profit surge 22.7 percent.

Operating profit climbed 15.2 percent to MXN$72,158 million, reflecting stronger underlying efficiency.

Accumulated EBITDA for the first six months reached MXN$119,022 million, the highest first-half level since 2018.

Mexico City. State utility CFE reported a 43% Q2 profit drop. (Photo: internal archive)

First-Half Profit Snapshot

The second-quarter currency shock pulled down the cumulative six-month figures.

First-half net profit totaled MXN$46,072.6 million, a decline of 31.7 percent compared to the first half of 2025.

The results highlight a bifurcated reality for the state enterprise: improving operations but vulnerable finances.

For international investors, this dynamic is a key risk to monitor when assessing Mexico’s broader fiscal health.

CFE and Pemex: The Twin Fiscal Drags

Credit rating agencies have long flagged CFE and Petróleos Mexicanos (Pemex), the state oil company, as contingent liabilities for Mexico’s sovereign credit rating.

Both entities are heavily indebted and operationally challenged, requiring periodic government support.

Fitch Ratings and other agencies view the financial health of these state-owned enterprises as directly linked to the government’s fiscal strength.

A severe deterioration at either company could pressure Mexico’s sovereign rating, raising borrowing costs for the country.

CFE’s foreign-exchange-driven profit swing underscores how external shocks can quickly strain its balance sheet.

The government relies on CFE to provide electricity to nearly the entire nation, making its financial stability a matter of public policy.

What This Means for International Investors

For expatriates and foreign investors in Mexico, CFE’s results are a reminder of how currency volatility transmits through state finances.

A weaker peso can erode the dollar value of local earnings while simultaneously inflating the debt burden of state-owned firms.

Investors holding Mexican government bonds or considering infrastructure exposure should track CFE’s debt profile closely.

The utility’s improving operational margins are a positive signal, but they remain vulnerable to exchange-rate swings.

Any sovereign downgrade linked to CFE or Pemex could trigger capital outflows and peso depreciation, creating a feedback loop.

The government has so far maintained explicit and implicit guarantees for both companies, but the fiscal cost is rising.

Looking Ahead: Debt Management and the Peso

CFE’s management has not announced new hedging strategies, but the second-quarter shock may renew focus on liability management.

The company’s ability to refinance dollar debt into peso obligations depends on domestic market depth and investor appetite.

Mexico’s central bank, Banco de México, maintains a cautious monetary policy stance that influences the peso’s trajectory.

A stabilization or appreciation of the peso in the second half could reverse some of the foreign-exchange losses.

However, global factors, including US interest rate policy and risk appetite, will largely determine the exchange rate.

For now, CFE remains a fundamentally strong operator with a balance sheet highly sensitive to currency markets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did CFE’s profit drop so sharply in Q2 2026?

CFE’s net profit fell 43.4% primarily because of a sharp decrease in foreign-exchange gains. With 52% of its debt in foreign currency, a weaker peso increased the local-currency value of its dollar obligations, creating a significant accounting loss.

How did CFE’s operations perform despite the profit decline?

Operational metrics improved significantly. First-half gross profit rose 22.7%, operating profit increased 15.2%, and EBITDA reached MXN$119,022 million, the highest first-half level since 2018, driven by an 8.4% reduction in cost of sales.

Why are rating agencies concerned about CFE?

Agencies like Fitch view CFE and Pemex as contingent liabilities for Mexico’s sovereign rating. Their high debt levels and vulnerability to external shocks, such as currency depreciation, could force the government to provide financial support, straining public finances.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief July 31 — North America is jangling with a mix of anger, defiance and fatigue as a 35% tariff hammer falls on Canadian goods and the region faces rising security fears. A newly elected Canadian government pledges immediate retaliation while communities also grapple with a deadly Montreal shooting and devastating wildfires.

The mood is one of confrontation on the trade front and deep watchfulness at home.

USA – Middle East security tensions

U.S. forces intercept reported Iranian attack

U.S. forces intercepted a reported Iranian ‘surprise attack’ targeting American troops early Friday, raising fears of a wider Middle East conflict. Washington is now weighing military options against Iran, though none are considered low-risk.

Recent strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq, Iranian targeting of U.S. force sites in Jordan, and a U.S.-owned ship hit in an Egyptian port are feeding into political and defence calculations. The simmering tensions add a layer of national-security anxiety to an already jittery American mood.

Canada – Wildfires and extreme weather

BC resort wrecked, Alberta tornado strikes

Intense wildfire activity in British Columbia destroyed cabins and trailers at a resort in Boston Bar, with the owner describing ‘wreckage everywhere.’ The fires are adding to provincial emergency-management and insurance burdens while producing cross-border smoke.

In Alberta, a tornado touched down at a campground, sending three people to hospital and damaging property. The severe weather pattern is compounding a sense of vulnerability across Canadian communities already stressed by economic and security shocks.

North America is on edge — a sharp tariff escalation is reopening the raw bilateral trade wound from 2025.

The Bigger Picture A single presidential signature early Friday shoved the Canada-U.S. trade relationship into a harsher chapter, lifting tariffs to 35% and drawing an immediate midnight vow of retaliation from Prime Minister Carney. The economic blow lands on autos, farms and factories, while Ottawa races to accelerate a diversification strategy built over the past year. At the same time, U.S. forces intercepted an Iranian attack and are weighing risky military options, deepening the sense of a White House governing by disruption on multiple fronts. The security picture is further darkened at home by a deadly Montreal shooting being treated as a serious incident. Canadian communities are also battling nature’s onslaught, with wildfires devouring a BC resort and a tornado hospitalising three people in Alberta. Across North America, the mood is a volatile mix of confrontation, watchfulness and weary defiance.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief July 31: What We Are Watching

Today – Immediate Canadian retaliatory tariff announcement and sector-support package expected.

This week – FIFA World Cup 2026 matches across the USA, Canada and Mexico amid strained trilateral relations.

Go Deeper The full USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier — the interactive risk dashboard, the six people who matter and the downloadable PDF — is updated daily by the Rio Times Intelligence Desk.

The USA & Canada Intelligence Brief July 31 returns tomorrow morning.

What drives the differences between the Rio Times brief and verified facts

The Rio Times brief treats the 35% tariff as a new July 31, 2026 event, but verified research shows that increase from 25% to 35% actually occurred on August 1, 2025 under an IEEPA executive order.

The real July 2026 development is the announcement of new 50% tariffs on roughly US$20 billion of Canadian goods, signed July 20 and scheduled to take effect August 19, 2026 under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

According to Bank of Canada estimates from July 15, 2026, the average US tariff on Canadian imports currently sits at roughly 5.0%, while Canada’s average tariff on US imports is about 1.5%, neither figure yet reflecting the announced 50% hike.

Hidden trade costs foreigners consistently underestimate

Foreign businesses often assume USMCA compliance guarantees duty-free access, but the July 2026 Section 338 announcement deliberately targets USMCA-compliant goods, covering items from wine and hockey sticks to cement, dairy products, furniture, and clothing.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on US steel, aluminum, and non-USMCA-compliant vehicles remain active even after most counter-tariffs were removed in September 2025, creating a patchwork where some goods face steep duties on both sides.

The US decision on July 1, 2026 not to extend the USMCA beyond its current term introduces long-term planning uncertainty for anyone building supply chains or distribution networks that depend on predictable North American trade rules.

How to choose a Latin American city for your budget

With nearly CAD$3.6 billion in daily Canada-US trade facing disruption, some foreign entrepreneurs and remote workers are evaluating Latin American alternatives, where tariff exposure and cost structures differ sharply by country and trade agreement.

Start by checking whether your target country has a ratified free trade agreement with your home market and the US, as Mexico’s USMCA membership offers duty advantages that most South American nations cannot match without separate bilateral deals.

Monthly living costs for a single person in mid-tier Latin American cities can range from roughly US$1,200 to US$2,500, but always verify local inflation figures and currency stability, since sudden devaluations can rapidly shift purchasing power in either direction.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are the 50% US tariffs on Canadian goods already in effect?

No, the 50% tariffs announced July 20, 2026 under Section 338 are scheduled to take effect 30 days after signing, meaning August 19, 2026, unless blocked legally or renegotiated before that date.

Does USMCA membership still protect Canadian goods from all US tariffs?

No, the existing 35% tariff from 2025 applies to non-USMCA-compliant goods, and the new July 2026 Section 338 tariffs explicitly target USMCA-compliant products including wine, dairy, furniture, and clothing, with only energy, potash, certain fish, and critical minerals carved out.

What retaliatory tariffs does Canada currently impose on US imports?

As of July 2026, Canada retains tariffs on US steel, aluminum, and a 25% duty on US vehicles that fail to meet USMCA rules of origin, while most other retaliatory tariffs were removed in September 2025.

Will the USMCA trade agreement be extended beyond its current term?

On July 1, 2026, the United States declined to extend the agreement for another 16 years, so USMCA remains in force but moves forward without a guaranteed long-term renewal, according to verified reporting.

Scorching temperatures and post-victory riots are straining emergency services, just as political bombshells in Spain, Germany, and France redefine the continent’s near future.

Spain – Corruption Verdict

A trusted ally falls

Spain’s Supreme Court has sentenced José Luis Ábalos, a former transport minister and close ally of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, to 24 years in prison for corruption.

The case centred on the awarding of inflated contracts for medical supplies during the COVID-19 pandemic, landing a devastating blow on the Socialist leader’s fragile coalition.

A government already hanging by a thread

The verdict fuels a deep sense of cynical anger across the country, sullying a prime minister who depends on razor-thin parliamentary support from smaller parties.

The political shock comes as emergency crews are already stretched thin by a dangerous heatwave and wildfires, leaving the government scrambling to contain the damage on multiple fronts.

Germany – Defence Procurement

A historic missile deal

Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed a landmark agreement with the United States to purchase long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles and station them on German soil for the first time.

The move significantly extends Germany’s strike reach and signals a proud new chapter in its military posture, though it is tinged with underlying public anxiety.

Kremlin promises retaliation

The Kremlin reacted with immediate fury, labelling the deployment a direct threat to Russian security and pledging a military response to what it called an escalation.

The bold German step is likely to eclipse discussions of economic ties when EU finance ministers meet in Brussels, reframing the bloc’s relationship with Moscow.

This is a nation forced to choose, in 48 hours, between swallowing a budget it hates or facing a chaotic governmental void.

Ukraine – A Long War of Attrition

Largest drone strike yet

President Volodymyr Zelensky oversaw and publicised the largest long-range drone strike of the war, setting Russian oil infrastructure alight and hitting logistical targets inside occupied Crimea.

The operation brought a surge of defiant satisfaction in Kyiv, paired with the grim understanding that this remains a gruelling war of attrition.

The Bigger Picture Europe is gripped by a suffocating blend of literal and political heat, with a record-shattering heatwave contributing to thousands of deaths, concentrated in France, Spain, and Belgium. A Spanish corruption verdict has wounded the prime minister’s inner circle, Germany has dramatically reoriented its defence posture with a Tomahawk missile deal, and the French government is gambling its survival on a contested budget pushed through by decree. Even historic diplomatic moves, like Macron’s surprise visit to Syria, feel like crisis management, as Poland teeters on early elections and Ukraine prosecutes a long war of attrition while European cities remain under red alert for dangerous temperatures.

Europe Intelligence Brief July 31: What We Are Watching

Today – The 24-hour window for France’s opposition to file a no-confidence motion expires, potentially toppling the government, while red heat alerts persist.

This week – EU finance ministers gather in Brussels for the ECOFIN Council to discuss fiscal rules, the French budget crisis, and the economic impact of the German missile deal.

What Drives the Differences Between Headlines and Verified Facts

The Rio Times brief often summarizes complex European legal and political developments using compressed language that can blur timing or finality, according to the verified research.

For example, the Ábalos sentence is a real Supreme Court decision, but the research notes it is not breaking news for July 31, while other claims about German missile basing decisions were not found in any primary European news sources at that time.

Hidden Costs Foreigners Underestimate When Following European Crises

Political instability headlines, such as France forcing a budget without a vote or a Polish president threatening early elections, can trigger sudden currency swings that erode the value of savings held in euros or local bank accounts.

Corruption scandals like the Ábalos mask contracts lead to tighter EU public procurement rules, which increase compliance costs and legal fees for any Latin American company exporting medical supplies or pharmaceuticals into Europe.

How to Choose a City for Your Budget

A record heatwave with red alerts and temperatures above 40°C has killed thousands across France and Spain, so your budget must account for higher seasonal air-conditioning and health insurance costs in southern cities.

Political deadlock in key NATO members like Poland can delay infrastructure projects and create processing backlogs for residence permits, meaning you need a larger emergency fund to cover living costs during administrative waits.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was the Ábalos corruption sentence a new event on July 31?

The Rio Times brief lists it as breaking news, but verified research shows the Spanish Supreme Court’s 24-year sentence for pandemic mask contract corruption was already a settled decision by that date.

Did Germany announce it would station American Tomahawk missiles on July 31?

The specific claim from the Rio Times brief could not be verified in any primary European news wires; the day’s coverage instead focused on migration crises in Ceuta and a missile incident in Poland.

How does the European heatwave affect a foreigner’s cost of living?

Red alerts across France and Spain with deadly temperatures above 40°C mean you must budget for higher electricity bills from constant air-conditioning and potentially higher health insurance premiums during extreme weather events.

What legal risks do Latin American exporters face after the Ábalos mask scandal?

EU members are now imposing stricter due-diligence and transparency checks on public health contracts, creating higher compliance costs for Latin American medical suppliers but also a more level playing field against corrupt intermediaries.

ASEAN – Manila Summit Tackles Dual Crises

Diplomatic scramble amid war fears

ASEAN foreign ministers opened a three-day summit in Manila on Friday with a heavy agenda dominated by the Iran war and the simmering South China Sea confrontation.

Ministers plan to issue a joint statement calling for an immediate Middle East ceasefire and the safe reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil artery for the region.

A region holding its breath

The mood inside the meetings matched the exhaustion and brittle anxiety felt across Asian capitals, with diplomats trying to contain economic spillover from a conflict half a world away.

The gathering played out against an emotional backdrop in the host nation, where rescue workers were still digging through the mud left by Storm Trami.

Region – Sanctions Relief Offers Energy Hope

60-day window opens for Asian buyers

In a rare piece of constructive news for energy importers, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control has issued General License X, a 60-day authorisation covering the production, sale and delivery of Iranian crude, petroleum products and petrochemicals.

The move would allow key Asian buyers to resume purchases of Iranian crude under a broader peace framework, offering some relief to markets rattled by instability.

Asia is on edge today, as a flicker of hope from a US-brokered India-Pakistan ceasefire was immediately extinguished by a missile strike.

India – Generation Z Marches on Parliament

Youth anger boils over

Defiance and anger filled the streets of Delhi as Generation Z protesters marched toward India’s Parliament, demanding the Education Minister resign over a lack of livelihood opportunities.

The domestic turmoil unfolded even as the Indian military exchanged fire with Pakistan, adding a layer of social pressure to the security crisis facing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.

The Bigger Picture A brief India–Pakistan ceasefire collapsed and missile strikes landed, stoking fears of a wider conflict and triggering a historic slide in shares across Asia. In Manila, Southeast Asian foreign ministers are attempting to project unity by demanding an end to the Iran war and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. A temporary US decision to ease Iranian oil sanctions offers Asian energy buyers a short breathing spell, but it remains a fragile lifeline tied to an uncertain peace process. In Delhi, young protesters challenged the Modi government on economic grievances, while Bangladesh saw its prime minister flee and a court order the release of her jailed rival overnight.

Today – India-Pakistan tensions after the ceasefire collapsed into fresh missile strikes.

How to Choose a City for Your Budget Amid Asia-Linked Volatility

Check whether your target city relies heavily on imported LNG or oil products from the Middle East, because prolonged Strait of Hormuz closures raise local utility costs unevenly across the region.

Monitor ASEAN–China energy cooperation updates on power interconnectivity and civilian nuclear expansion, as these signal which cities may stabilize electricity prices faster during oil price spikes.

Did the India–Pakistan ceasefire really collapse on July 31?

In Manila, ASEAN’s July 2026 joint statements call for an immediate cessation of Middle East hostilities and safe, unimpeded transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

World.content:

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Bar Brahma A legendary corner of São Paulo where samba and MPB ring out live every Friday. Go for the history, stay for the dancing crowd that spills onto Avenida São João.

Tonight at a Glance —Bar Brahma Historic samba and MPB house in Centro; mixed crowd of locals and visitors; Friday live music from 9 pm. —Tokyo Marine Hall Big-stage Friday show with Péricles spinning pagode gold; romantic, singalong energy; arrive by 10 pm. —D-Edge World-class electronic club in Barra Funda; international DJs and a serious sound system; after midnight. —Casa Fluida LGBTQ+ house and garden party in Bela Vista; warm queer crowd; Friday nights are for mingling and DJ sets. —Boteco Rainha Vila Madalena boteco with choro circles and cold beer; perfect to start the night; expat-friendly, arrive 8 pm.

Friday night in São Paulo stretches from a cold beer at 8 pm in Vila Madalena to a warehouse rave in Barra Funda at 5 am. Our picks for 31 July 2026 mix live samba legends, pagode singalongs, deep electronic sets and a queer garden party.

São Paulo after dark: the city’s nightlife stretches across entire districts. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Couvert Artístico: live MPB, samba and choro with rotating musicians — at Bar Brahma, from 9 pm. The classic Friday night soundtrack in Centro. A beer, a pastel and live Brazilian music in a room full of history.

Péricles ao vivo – pagode and romantic samba — at Tokyo Marine Hall, doors 9 pm, show around 10:30 pm. One of Brazil’s great modern pagode voices in a proper concert setting. High-energy, full-band singalong.

D-Edge Friday: resident and guest DJs (house and techno) — at D-Edge, from midnight. A temple of Brazilian electronic music with a flawless sound system and a queer-friendly, music-first dance floor.

Sexta Fluida – DJ sets and garden social — at Casa Fluida, from 9 pm. The best Friday house party for São Paulo’s queer crowd and their friends. Easy to meet people early in the garden.

Choro and samba de raiz circle — at Boteco Rainha, from 7:30 pm. A proper Vila Madalena start: cold beer, cachaça and acoustic choro before the night gets big.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm up (8 pm–11 pm): Vila Madalena and Pinheiros botecos for cold beer, choro and early conversation. Bar Brahma in Centro also works as a first stop.

Prime time (11 pm–2 am): live samba and MPB sets peak. Larger shows like Péricles at Tokyo Marine Hall run their main set.

Bars on Rua Augusta get lively.

After midnight (12 am–4 am): clubs hit their stride. D-Edge and other Barra Funda spaces open deep into the night.

The queer scene gathers at Casa Fluida and Bela Vista parties.

Late late (4 am–6 am): a few after-hours spots and street eats around Baixo Augusta and Barra Funda. Uber and 99 are your only safe rides home.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba and Pagode — Roots samba and romantic pagode with big live bands. Dancing, cold beer and tables full of friends. Where: Bar Brahma (Centro), Tokyo Marine Hall (shows), Boteco Rainha (Vila Madalena)

Electronic — House, techno and Brazilian bass on crisp sound systems in dark, serious rooms or warehouse spaces. Where: D-Edge (Barra Funda), Carlos Capslock (Bixiga), ODD (Barra Funda)

MPB and Choro — Brazilian popular music and instrumental choro in small, attentive rooms or lively bar corners. Where: Bar Brahma, Casa de Francisca (Jardins), Ó do Borogodó (Pinheiros)

LGBTQ+ and Pop — Queer parties with pop, disco and Brazilian divas; some in clubs, some in house-and-garden settings. Where: Casa Fluida (Bela Vista), Zig Club (Consolação), Bubu Lounge (Pinheiros)

Forró — Northeastern forró dancing with live trios; beginner-friendly and partner-dancing heavy. Where: Remelexo (Vila Madalena), Canto da Ema (Pinheiros)

Sertanejo — Brazilian country pop with big-production shows and a young, well-dressed crowd. Where: Villa Country (Barra Funda), shows at Vibra São Paulo and Espaço Unimed

Pick Your Night

Date night: Casa de Francisca in Jardins for intimate MPB shows and candlelit tables. Reserve ahead.

Solo and safe: Bar Brahma early (before 10 pm) then move to D-Edge after midnight.

Dance till sunrise: D-Edge or a Barra Funda warehouse party.

Meet locals: Boteco Rainha in Vila Madalena early, then any Friday pagode show.

Chill and conversation: Ó do Borogodó in Pinheiros.

Meet other expats: Any Friday happy hour in Baixo Pinheiros or a language-exchange night at a pub like O’Malleys.

Where to Go

Bar Brahma — Centro One of the city's great music rooms. A classic aviation-themed bar with live samba, MPB and choro. Mixed crowd of all ages. Tonight: Couvert artístico with live samba and MPB from 9 pm. A reliable Friday standby. Best time: Friday and Saturday nights from 9 pm. Arrive before 9:30 pm to get a good table. Cost: Couvert artístico around R$30–R$50. Beer from R$15. Card and cash accepted. Address: Avenida São João, 677, Centro Phone: +55 11 3367-3600 Instagram: @barbrahmacentro Website: www.barbrahma.com.br Getting there: Metrô República (red line). Use Uber or 99 to the door; do not wander the surrounding streets late. Good to know: Book a table via the website, especially for groups. No strict door rule; smart casual is fine.

D-Edge — Barra Funda São Paulo's most famous electronic club. Three dance floors, a crisp Funktion-One sound system and serious DJ bookings. Music-first crowd, very welcoming queer presence. Tonight: Friday night house and techno with resident and guest DJs. Doors midnight. Best time: Fridays and Saturdays from midnight. Arrive around 1 am when the floor is filling up. Cost: Entry R$40–R$120 depending on the night. Beer around R$15–R$18. Card accepted. Comanda system at the door. Address: Avenida Auro Soares de Moura Andrade, 141, Barra Funda Phone: +55 11 3665-9500 Instagram: @dedge Website: www.d-edge.com.br Getting there: Metrô Marechal Deodoro (blue line) or Barra Funda (red line). Safe by Uber; the street outside is quiet but the venue-run queue is secure. Good to know: Buy tickets online via Sympla or at the door. No dress code; black and understated is common. Bring ID.

Casa Fluida — Bela Vista A house-turned-garden party space that is the beating heart of São Paulo’s alternative queer scene. DJ sets, cocktails and a crowd that talks as much as it dances. Tonight: Sexta Fluida party from 9 pm with resident DJs and a garden bar. Best time: Friday nights. Arrive early (9 pm–10 pm) to enjoy the garden and meet people while it is still conversational. Cost: Entry R$30–R$50. Drinks R$15–R$25. Card and cash. Comanda system likely. Address: Rua Rocha, 286, Bela Vista Instagram: @casafluida Getting there: Walkable from Avenida Paulista. Uber is easiest; pickup right outside is safe as the street is residential but active. Good to know: No reservation needed; arrive early. Welcoming, no dress code. Respect the space’s queer foundation.

Boteco Rainha — Vila Madalena A tiny, beloved boteco with plastic tables on the pavement, cold beer and spontaneous choro circles. The crowd is a genuine mix of students, musicians and neighbourhood locals. Tonight: Informal choro and samba de raiz from early evening. The music starts organically around 7:30 pm. Best time: Any evening from 7 pm, especially Thursday to Saturday. Arrive by 8 pm to grab a pavement table. Cost: No couvert; beer from R$10. Cash preferred; some cards accepted. Pay per drink. Address: Rua Inácio Pereira da Rocha, 388, Vila Madalena Instagram: @botecorainha.oficial Getting there: Metrô Vila Madalena (green line), then a short walk or a quick Uber. The street corner is lively and safe. Good to know: No bookings; first-come for tables. Super casual; shorts and trainers are perfect.

Tokyo Marine Hall — Liberdade A polished mid-size concert hall that books some of Brazil’s best loved pagode, samba and MPB artists. Excellent sound and sightlines; feels like a proper show. Tonight: Péricles live pagode show. Doors 9 pm, main set around 10:30 pm. Best time: Programmed show nights, typically Friday and Saturday. Arrive by 10 pm. Cost: Tickets from R$80 via Sympla. Drinks inside at concert-bar prices. Card accepted. Address: Rua Galvão Bueno, 366, Liberdade Phone: +55 11 3207-7111 Instagram: @tokyomarinehall Website: www.tokyomarinehall.com.br Getting there: Metrô São Joaquim (blue line) or Liberdade (blue line). The area is busy after shows; Uber and 99 are easy from the door. Good to know: Buy tickets in advance on Sympla; shows frequently sell out. Smart casual dress.

Ó do Borogodó — Pinheiros A small, candlelit temple of samba where the music is the star. Intimate room with excellent musicians and a grown-up, listening crowd. Tonight: Live samba and gafieira dancing roster varies weekly. A reliable, cosy Friday standby. Best time: Friday and Saturday; music from around 9:30 pm. Arrive by 9 pm for a seat. Cost: Couvert artístico R$25–R$40. Caipirinhas from R$20. Card and cash accepted. Address: Rua Horácio Lane, 21, Pinheiros Phone: +55 11 3814-4087 Instagram: @odoborogodo Website: www.odoborogodo.com.br Getting there: Near Metrô Fradique Coutinho (yellow line). A short, safe walk or a cheap Uber from the station. Good to know: Table booking recommended via WhatsApp. Door is relaxed; just come for the music.

Casa de Francisca — Jardins An elegant, hushed room for live MPB and instrumental music. Excellent food, a serious whisky and cocktail list, and a date-night atmosphere. Tonight: Programmed MPB or instrumental show (check Instagram for the week’s artist). Shows from 9:30 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday. Shows start at 9:30 pm; arrive by 8:30 pm for dinner. Cost: Show ticket R$60–R$100. Dinner and drinks extra. Card accepted. Reservations strongly advised. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva, 22, Jardins Phone: +55 11 2615-0192 Instagram: @casadefrancisca Website: www.casadefrancisca.com.br Getting there: Near Avenida Paulista and Metrô Brigadeiro (green line). Clean, safe Jardins location; easy Uber access. Good to know: Book a table online or via WhatsApp. Smart dress; no sportswear. Quiet talking during sets.

Zig Club — Consolação A three-floor LGBTQ+ club on Rua Augusta. Pop, funk and diva anthems across different rooms. Young, energetic and very Brazilian. Tonight: Friday night pop and drag performances. Doors from 11 pm. Best time: Fridays and Saturdays from midnight. Arrive around 12:30 am; the club peaks late. Cost: Entry R$30–R$80. Comanda card system. Drinks from R$15. Card accepted. Address: Rua Augusta, 523, Consolação Instagram: @zigclub Website: www.zigclub.com.br Getting there: Near Metrô Consolação (green line). Rua Augusta is active; use Uber or 99 from the door. Good to know: Buy tickets online. ID required. The door is friendly; come as you are.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Vila Madalena: Bohemian and bar-dense, with boteco tables spilling onto every pavement. Young creatives, students and a strong expat presence.

Pinheiros: The slicker, foodier sibling of Vila Madalena. Great small music rooms, craft cocktails and a professional crowd.

Baixo Augusta: The strip from Paulista to Centro is an alternative artery of rock bars, LGBTQ+ clubs, neon and people-watching.

Barra Funda: Industrial-scale clubs, big concerts and underground parties in converted warehouses. Spread out, best reached by Uber.

Centro: Historic bars, samba houses and old São Paulo soul around República and Avenida São João. Go for the music, stay sharp on quiet side streets.

Liberdade: Japanese-Brazilian neighbourhood by day, with a small pocket of mid-size concert halls and karaoke bars lighting up at night.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Casa Fluida — A warm garden party and house in Bela Vista. Queer-run, mixed crowd, easy conversations and DJ sets. Friday is the night.

Zig Club — Big, loud and proudly poppy LGBTQ+ club on Rua Augusta. Three floors of music, drag shows and a young, inclusive crowd.

D-Edge — Not exclusively LGBTQ+ but a famously queer-friendly electronic music club with a mixed, respectful crowd and a safe dance floor.

Money & How Paying Works The comanda card system: at the door you get a tab card. Every drink goes on it. You pay the total at the cashier on exit. Losing the card means a heavy fine, often R$150 or more. Couvert artístico: a live-music cover charge added to your bill in samba and MPB houses. Usually R$15–R$40 per person and not optional once music has started. Payment: credit and debit cards are widely accepted, even for small amounts. Carry some cash for tiny botecos and street vendors. Tipping: a 10% service charge is normally included. No need to add more, though rounding up for great service is appreciated.

Getting Home Safe

The Metrô closes around midnight. Do not plan your journey around a late train home.

Check the station times if you plan to leave before 11:30 pm.

Use Uber or the 99 app for trips after dark. Cars arrive in minutes and you track the whole route with GPS.

Order your ride from inside the bar or club. Step out only when the driver has arrived and you can see the licence plate on your screen.

Stick to busy, well-lit streets in Centro and around empty stretches of Avenida Paulista. Vila Madalena and Pinheiros feel safer simply because they are packed until late.

Keep your phone and wallet out of sight when walking. A quick check inside a bar or a corner shop is fine; scrolling on a dark pavement is not.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time should I really go out on a Friday in São Paulo?

Start bars at 8 or 9 pm. Live music peaks around 10:30 pm.

Clubs only fill up after midnight. Arriving to a club before 11:30 pm can feel very quiet.

Do I need to speak Portuguese to enjoy the night?

Not in the big rooms. English is understood in Pinheiros, larger clubs and tourist-friendly spots.

A few words of Portuguese will open doors and smiles everywhere else.

Is São Paulo safe for a solo foreigner at night?

Yes, if you use common sense. Stay in popular neighbourhoods, use Uber to move between stops, and protect your phone.

The warmth of a good samba circle makes the city feel small.

World.title: Novak Djokovic Returns to Cincinnati With US Open History at Stake
World.content:
Novak Djokovic will return to the Cincinnati Open in August, choosing one final hard-court tournament before resuming his pursuit of a record 25th Grand Slam singles title at the US Open. The 39-year-old Serbian is part of the Cincinnati field after withdrawing from the Canadian Open in Montreal to manage his workload. His decision gives him additional recovery time following Wimbledon while still providing an opportunity to test his form before the season’s final major.



The Cincinnati Open runs from August 8 through August 23. The US Open begins August 23, with the singles main draws starting August 30 in New York. Djokovic’s appearance will mark his return to a tournament where he has produced some of the most memorable tennis of his career.

He is a three-time Cincinnati champion, winning the event in 2018, 2020 and 2023. His most recent title came after a remarkable final against Carlos Alcaraz that lasted three hours and 49 minutes. Djokovic saved a championship point before defeating Alcaraz 5-7, 7-6(7), 7-6(4). The match remains the longest best-of-three-set final in ATP Tour history.

Cincinnati now carries a different kind of importance for Djokovic. He remains capable of reaching the closing stages of the sport’s biggest tournaments, but winning them has become increasingly difficult as Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have taken control of the men’s game.

Djokovic reached the Australian Open final in February after defeating Sinner in a five-set semifinal. Alcaraz then denied him the title in four sets, becoming the first player to defeat Djokovic in an Australian Open final.

At Wimbledon, Djokovic survived a five-hour, 15-minute quarterfinal against Félix Auger-Aliassime before losing to Sinner in the semifinals. It was another strong Grand Slam run, but it also illustrated the physical challenge facing Djokovic when he must defeat several leading players over two weeks.

“It’s good, but not good enough,” Djokovic said after his Wimbledon exit. His reduced schedule reflects that reality. Djokovic has increasingly avoided tournaments that might leave him physically depleted before the Grand Slams, preferring longer training periods and carefully selected appearances.

That strategy allows him to arrive rested, but it can also leave him short of competitive matches. Cincinnati offers a compromise. It gives Djokovic a high-level hard-court test against many of the same players he could face in New York, while leaving time to recover before the US Open singles competition begins.

The tournament will feature a deep men’s field led by Sinner, Alcaraz and several other leading contenders. Alcaraz won the Cincinnati title in 2025, while Sinner captured the championship in 2024. Djokovic enters the event ranked No. 5, meaning his path could include an earlier meeting with one of the tournament’s leading seeds.

The expanded Cincinnati format also makes recovery between matches and management of the summer heat important parts of any title run. The immediate objective will be finding his timing on outdoor hard courts. The larger question is whether he can still defeat Sinner or Alcaraz late in a major after navigating several demanding rounds.

Djokovic has not won a Grand Slam singles title since the 2023 US Open, when he collected his 24th major. He has continued reaching finals and semifinals since then, but the record-breaking 25th title has remained out of reach. Cincinnati will not settle that pursuit. It will, however, provide the clearest indication yet of whether Djokovic is ready for another serious challenge in New York.

World.title: International News: ICE Airport arrests raise alarm as Immigration Enforcement intensifies across US
World.content:
International News: ICE Airport arrests raise alarm as Immigration Enforcement intensifies across US

By Zoila Palma: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests at US airports are reportedly becoming more frequent, raising concerns among immigration attorneys who say travelers are increasingly being detained while attempting to board flights.

The arrests come as the agency faces pressure to advance President Donald Trump’s deportation agenda, including a stated goal of approximately 2,000 arrests per day, CNN reports.

Attorneys say the enforcement actions are increasingly targeting people with expired visas and others involved in immigration proceedings. In one recent case, a woman who had entered the United States legally and was seeking asylum was detained at a Washington, DC-area airport while traveling home to Texas for her father’s funeral. Another client represented by attorney Joe Moravec was reportedly detained at a Chicago airport despite also being legally present in the country.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has defended its enforcement approach, saying the administration is working to prevent undocumented immigrants from flying unless they are leaving the country voluntarily.

Immigration attorney Jeff Joseph, president of the American Immigration Lawyers Association, said the level of enforcement and cooperation between TSA and ICE at airports is unlike anything previously seen.

Former acting ICE Director John Sandweg said airports provide agents with a secure environment where travelers’ information and movements are already known, making arrests easier to carry out with fewer personnel.

World.title: Police Youth Cadet summer camp highlights discipline, leadership and youth talent
World.content:
Police Youth Cadet summer camp highlights discipline, leadership and youth talent

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department continued its youth-focused programming on Thursday, July 30, with Day 4 of the National Police Youth Cadet Corps Summer Camp 2026, featuring a day of competition, leadership development and talent showcases.

The activities included a Foot Drill Competition, where regional teams demonstrated discipline, teamwork, precision and coordination while performing various drill movements and reciting the Belize Police Youth Cadet Corps Pledge. The Northern Region emerged as champions, while the Eastern Region placed second.

The competition was adjudicated by Dangriga Town Mayor Robert Mariano, retired Police Inspector Matthew Lopez and Commander of the Community Oriented Policing Unit, Senior Superintendent Gerald Jones.

The Police Department said the event sought not only to test the cadets’ ability to perform drill movements accurately and in synchronization, but also to instill values including respect, responsibility, perseverance, leadership, compassion, morale and good sportsmanship.

The day’s activities concluded with the Cadet Glamorous Pageant Night, celebrating the creativity, confidence and talents of Belize’s youth. Cadets competed in segments including casual wear, talent showcase, formal No. 1 cadet uniform and evening wear, with Athena Azueta of Roaring Creek, representing the Western Region, crowned the winner.

The summer camp is a flagship initiative of the Community Oriented Policing Unit aimed at strengthening trust and positive relationships between young people and police officers while developing skills in leadership, teamwork, communication and problem-solving.

World.title: Taiwan’s Medical students conduct clinical placement in Belize
World.content:
Taiwan’s Medical students conduct clinical placement in Belize

By Zoila Palma: Taiwan Ambassador to Belize Amino Chi met recently with Taiwanese medical students from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University—Bo Jang Chiou, Tian Qi Wang, and Yi Chan.

The medical students are conducting their clinical placement under the guidance of Antonio Coyoc, Regional Hospital Administrator of the Western Regional Hospital.

During the meeting, they shared their experiences working alongside local healthcare professionals, caring for patients, and learning from Belize’s healthcare system.

Ambassador Chi commended the students for their passion for public service and their dedication to improving the health and well-being of the Belizean people.

The Taiwan Embassy pledged to continue to promote medical cooperation with Belize and deepen bilateral partnership.

World.title: International News: Spain says mass migrant surge into Ceuta reversed as thousands return to Morocco
World.content:
International News: Spain says mass migrant surge into Ceuta reversed as thousands return to Morocco

By Zoila Palma: Spain says a massive surge of migrants into its North African enclave of Ceuta has been brought under control, with thousands of those who crossed the border reportedly returning voluntarily to Morocco.

Spanish authorities estimated that about 50,000 people entered the territory by land and sea since Thursday, while local officials put the figure as high as 60,000.

At least 19 bodies were reportedly recovered from the water, while Ceuta’s local government said the death toll could be as high as 34, Reuters report.

Moroccan security forces used batons and tear gas to disperse crowds gathered near border gates as authorities sought to prevent further crossings. Water cannon were also deployed, while the charred remains of vehicles could be seen following clashes. Spanish military vehicles were positioned along sections of the border, as several hundred migrants were seen returning through official checkpoints and openings in the fence, with some saying they lacked food and shelter in Ceuta.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited Ceuta on Friday and described the mass crossing as a “violation of Spain’s territorial sovereignty.” He said authorities were accelerating the repatriation of migrants who entered illegally, with Morocco cooperating in the process.

Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres suggested that a recent Supreme Court ruling restricting the summary return of migrants intercepted at sea may have contributed to the surge.

World.title: BELTRAIDE and Mexican Ambassador discuss opportunities for expanding economic cooperation
World.content:
BELTRAIDE and Mexican Ambassador discuss opportunities for expanding economic cooperation

By Zoila Palma: On July 30, 2026, BELTRAIDE met with Ana Luisa Vallejo Barba, Ambassador of Mexico to Belize, and Guillermo Alejandro Hernandez Salmeron of the Embassy of Mexico to discuss opportunities for expanding economic cooperation between our two countries.

Executive Director Ishmael Quiroz, Deputy Executive Director Monique Usher, and EXPORTBelize Manager Diana Hernandez engaged in productive discussions with the Ambassador and Hernandez on strengthening bilateral trade and investment, promoting BELTRAIDE’s investment opportunities, enhancing export opportunities for Belizean businesses, exploring technical assistance initiatives, advancing an Export to Mexico Workshop, supporting the upcoming Belize–Mexico Friendship Week, and identifying new avenues for greater collaboration.

Discussions also included opportunities for Mexican companies to share their expertise, technologies, and business best practices with Belizean enterprises, while fostering stronger business-to-business partnerships and creating mutually beneficial trade and investment opportunities for both countries.

BELTRAIDE expressed enthusiasm in strengthening the partnership with the Embassy of Mexico to advance trade, investment, innovation, and sustainable economic growth between Belize and Mexico.

World.title: Another bicycle stolen from an Orange Walk yard overnight
World.content:
Another bicycle stolen from an Orange Walk yard overnight

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The bicycle thieves of the Orange Walk District have struck again, this time slipping into an unfenced Trial Farm yard in the dead of night and riding off with a beach cruiser while its owner slept.

According to the Belize Police Department, a man of the Trial Farm area visited the Trial Farm Police Station on Monday, July 27, 2026, to report the theft.

He told police that while he was sleeping at about 12:05 a.m., a man entered his unfenced yard and stole his Hurricane brand beach cruiser bicycle, which cost him $125.

Police recorded a statement from the complainant, and the matter is under investigation. No one has been detained or charged.

The theft adds to a persistent string of bicycle thefts across the district in recent weeks, with beach cruisers proving a favourite target, taken from yards, doorsteps, and even the bus terminal. The pattern carries a simple caution for bicycle owners: an unsecured bike in an open yard rarely survives the night unwatched.

Anyone with information on the theft, or who has seen a Hurricane beach cruiser change hands under questionable circumstances, is asked to contact the Trial Farm police.

World.title: Farm theft solved within a day as police recover solar lights
World.content:
Farm theft solved within a day as police recover solar lights

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The solar lights that vanished from a Nuevo San Juan farm in the dead of night did not stay missing long, and neither did the case stay open.

The Belize Police Department reports that a 56-year-old farmer of the village left his farm on Monday night at about 11:30 p.m. with everything where it belonged: two black solar lights and their panel, worth $300, mounted to a post and to the small board and zinc house that anchors his property on the village outskirts.

By 5:00 a.m., the phone was ringing. A relative had noticed the lights gone, and the farmer’s own checks confirmed it. By 10:00 a.m. Tuesday, he was at the police station with a name in mind and a request for court action.

What followed was the kind of turnaround complainants dream about. Statements came from the farmer and a witness, the lights and panel were recovered and photographed for evidence, and police secured a warrant in the first instance. Jorge David Mendez, 24, a labourer of Nuevo San Juan Village, was formally arrested and charged with theft, meeting the caution with silence.

Mendez, as with anyone charged, holds the presumption of innocence unless and until the court rules otherwise.

On a farm, solar lights are not decoration, they are the watchman that never sleeps, guarding the toolshed and the yard through the long rural dark. Taking them steals the light and the security in one pull. This time, both came back, and the courts will sort the rest.

Reported at ten, recovered and charged by day’s end. Police work the way every village hopes to see it.

World.title: Phone snatched from truck seat while owner sat at the wheel
World.content:
Phone snatched from truck seat while owner sat at the wheel

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Guinea Grass Village farmer had his cell phone stolen from inside his own truck, snatched from the passenger seat while he sat behind the steering wheel, and police are seeking a man in connection with the brazen theft.

According to the Belize Police Department, the 67-year-old farmer reported that on Wednesday, July 29, 2026, at about 10:50 p.m., his pickup truck was parked in the parking lot of a store in the village. He was seated behind the steering wheel with his cell phone resting on the passenger seat when a man approached the vehicle from the passenger side, reached in for the phone with his right hand, and ran off with it.

The farmer shouted the man’s name, he told police, but the thief made good his escape.

The complainant said he clearly recognized the man, someone he has known since the man was a child growing up in the village, aided by sufficient light from a nearby street light, though he could not recall the clothing the man wore.

The stolen phone is a beige NEO brand smartphone valued at $215, with a transparent blue rubber case valued at $20, a total loss of $235. The farmer requested court action, and a statement was recorded.

Police have listed a person as wanted in connection with the theft. As he has not been detained or charged, his identity is being withheld pending charges.

The matter remains under investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Guinea Grass Sub Station or the Orange Walk police.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.
